title: Practice Test 6: Claude Certified Architect - Foundations
description:
60 unique scenario-based questions with another random selection of 4 out of 6 scenarios. Domain distribution matches official exam guide weightings. Topics include agentic loop implementation, MCP tool design, Claude Code configuration, structured output, and context window management.

Every question has been validated for technical accuracy and topic scope compliance. Detailed explanations with documentation references follow each question.

Prerequisite: Review the official exam guide and complete Anthropic's free certification preparation courses (or have equivalent hands-on experience).

prompt.question:
SCENARIO: You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate.

QUESTION: Company policy states the agent should normally offer a replacement before processing a refund, but may skip the offer when the customer explicitly insists on a refund. How should you implement this policy?
answers: Add a PreToolUse hook that blocks every "process_refund" call until a replacement has been offered.
Route all refund requests through "escalate_to_human" so a person decides whether to offer a replacement first.
Add a PostToolUse hook on the refund tool that flags any refund issued without a prior replacement offer.
State the guideline in the system prompt, since applying it correctly requires per-case judgment.
feedbacks: The problem is not that a hook was chosen. The problem is that this specific hook blocks with no condition: it blocks all refunds until a replacement has been offered. It gives no way to honor the policy's exception for customers who insist on a refund. As written, it would block valid refunds and contradict the policy it is meant to implement.

Escalating every refund to a human hands off work that the agent can handle. It would severely hurt the 80% first-contact resolution target. The agent is fully able to apply this policy when the policy is written as clear prompt guidance.

PostToolUse hooks run after the tool call has already executed, so the refund would already be processed by the time the hook fires. This hook only detects the problem after the fact. It has no influence on how the agent applies the policy during the conversation.

This policy is discretionary by design: it depends on judgment and on what the customer says. The agent must decide whether the customer has insisted on a refund before it skips the replacement offer. Prompt-based guidance is the right fit because it keeps the model's judgment about the context of each case. None of the other options captures the exception that is built into the policy.
prompt.explanation:
The main design decision is hooks versus prompts. The deciding factor is whether the mechanism matches the type of rule. A PreToolUse hook runs before a tool call executes and can block it deterministically (every time, with no model judgment involved). That is what you want for rules with financial or compliance consequences, such as a hard upper limit on refunds. Hooks are not limited to unconditional rules. They can implement conditional logic, modify a tool call's input, or return decisions like deny, ask, or defer. The hook proposed in this scenario has a specific flaw. It blocks every process_refund call until a replacement has been offered. This leaves no path for the policy's own exception: a customer who explicitly insists on a refund. If you encode this discretionary rule as a block on all refunds, the agent will break the policy it is supposed to enforce.

Recognizing the exception depends on reading the customer's intent in the conversation. For that reason, the simplest and most appropriate place for this rule is the system prompt. Anthropic's documentation states the difference directly: prompt files and system instructions are context, not enforced configuration, while hooks and permissions operate outside the prompt. Prompt guidance keeps the model's judgment about context active, and a rule of the form "normally do X, unless the customer says Y" needs that judgment. By contrast, "never refund above $500" needs no judgment and belongs in a PreToolUse hook.

The other approaches fail for different reasons. A PostToolUse hook fires only after a successful tool call, so the refund has already executed. It can send feedback back to the model, but it cannot prevent anything or change the order of anything. Routing every refund to escalate_to_human gives up automation for a task the agent handles well, and this directly harms the first-contact resolution goal. See Agent SDK Hooks and Modifying System Prompts for how these two mechanisms divide responsibility.

QUESTION: Billing disputes the agent handles vary widely: duplicate charges, missed discounts, overlapping subscriptions. The correct investigation steps only become clear after seeing the customer's account data. How should the agent plan its investigation?
answers: Define a fixed checklist of tool calls that every dispute follows in the same order.
Classify each dispute first and route it to one of several predefined tool pipelines.
Raise the loop's maximum turn limit so the agent can work through longer checklists.
Have the agent map the account state first, then generate subtasks from what it discovers.
feedbacks: A fixed pipeline fits tasks with a predictable structure, such as a review that always follows the same template. Billing disputes have different root causes. A single predefined sequence will run irrelevant steps on some cases and miss necessary steps on others.

Routing is better than a single checklist, but each branch is still a fixed plan. The agent commits to that plan before it gathers any evidence. The account data may reveal something the chosen pipeline did not expect, such as a second overlapping issue. When that happens, the agent cannot adjust its remaining steps.

A higher turn limit gives the agent more iterations, but it does not change what those iterations do. The real problem is that the plan is decided before the evidence exists. The problem is not that the agent runs out of turns.

This is dynamic adaptive decomposition. A first survey of the account establishes what is actually going on, and the agent then generates the next investigation steps from those findings. For open-ended work with high ambiguity, where the scope is unknown at the start, this pattern produces coverage that no predefined step list can match.
prompt.explanation:
This question contrasts the two documented task decomposition strategies. In fixed pipelines (prompt chaining), every step is listed in advance. In dynamic adaptive decomposition, the agent generates subtasks based on what it discovers at each step. The choice depends on predictability. When a task always follows the same structure, a fixed sequence gives stability and reproducible results. When the scope is unknown until evidence arrives, as with billing disputes that have high ambiguity, the plan itself must come out of the investigation. The agent surveys the account first and then derives the specific subtasks that the findings call for.

The Claude Agent SDK is built around this capability. Its agent loop feeds every tool result back to the model before the next decision. So a dispute that turns out to involve both a duplicate charge and an expired discount can create investigation steps for each, even though neither could be predicted when the request arrived. Anthropic's dynamic workflows documentation shows the same map-first pattern at a larger scale. A discovery step runs first, and one subtask is generated for each discovered item instead of from a hard-coded list.

The incorrect approaches all commit to a plan before evidence exists. A universal checklist wastes calls on irrelevant steps and leaves out necessary ones. An up-front routing classifier is a real technique, but it only selects among predefined pipelines. It cannot revise a plan during the investigation when the data turns out to be unexpected. Raising the turn limit addresses capacity, not planning. By default the loop has no turn limit at all, and more iterations of a wrong plan do not make it right.

QUESTION: After investigating a billing dispute, the main agent delegates drafting of the customer reply to a resolution-drafting subagent. The drafts repeatedly omit the dispute amounts and order IDs the main agent already retrieved. What change most effectively fixes this?
answers: Increase the subagent's context allocation so more of the parent conversation carries over into its window.
Grant the drafting subagent the backend MCP tools so it can re-query the customer and order data itself.
Add a system prompt instruction directing the subagent to consult the main agent's conversation history.
Pass the complete investigation findings, including amounts and order IDs, in the drafting subagent's prompt.
feedbacks: The problem is not context size. The parent conversation never enters the subagent's window at all, no matter how large that window is. A subagent starts fresh with only the prompt it is given, so a larger capacity changes nothing.

Fetching again the data that the main agent already retrieved adds redundant tool calls, latency, and cost. Without that context, the subagent may also not know which customer or orders to query. The investigation results already exist, and they should be passed in the delegation prompt.

A non-fork subagent has no access to the parent's conversation history. No instruction can make it consult content that is not in its context. Prompt wording cannot replace passing the findings explicitly.

Subagents run in an isolated context. They do not inherit the parent conversation or its tool results. The only content passed from parent to subagent is the prompt string. Including the complete findings directly in that prompt is the documented pattern. It guarantees that the drafting subagent has the amounts and order IDs it needs.
prompt.explanation:
In every multi-agent design, a subagent is a separate agent instance with an isolated context window. A non-fork subagent does not see the parent's conversation history, the parent's tool results, or files the parent already read. According to the Agent SDK documentation, the only content passed from parent to subagent is the prompt string given when the subagent is invoked. If the dispute amounts and order IDs are not in that prompt, the drafting subagent does not have them at all. That is why its replies come out generic.

This isolation is a deliberate tradeoff, not a limitation to work around. It keeps long investigation output (long tool results, intermediate reasoning) out of the contexts of later agents, and it lets each subagent keep a focused system prompt. The cost of that isolation is that context passing becomes the orchestrator's explicit responsibility. For sequential handoffs, the correct design is to include the complete relevant findings directly in the next subagent's task prompt, ideally in a structured form that separates data from metadata.

Each of the other approaches misses this. Giving the subagent the MCP tools makes it repeat work the main agent already completed. This uses extra tool calls and adds latency, and the subagent is still unsure which records to fetch. Telling it to consult the main conversation asks for something the architecture does not allow, because that history never enters its context. Enlarging the context allocation treats an isolation boundary as if it were a capacity problem.

See Subagents in the SDK and Create custom subagents for the full context-inheritance rules.

QUESTION: The team designs a coordinator agent that delegates billing-dispute investigation and order-history investigation to two separate subagents. Which two design decisions correctly reflect how this hub-and-spoke architecture works? (Select TWO.)
answers: Have the two subagents exchange messages directly with each other to reconcile any overlapping findings before reporting their results.
Rely on each subagent automatically inheriting the coordinator's full conversation history so case details never need restating when delegating.
Handle subagent failures in the coordinator, which decides whether to retry the task, delegate it again, or proceed with partial results.
Keep each subagent's intermediate tool calls and results isolated in its own context and have it return only a final report to the coordinator.
feedbacks: This is incorrect. In the subagent model, all results return to the calling agent, and subagents have no channel to send messages to one another. Direct messaging between peers is a feature of the separate, experimental agent teams mode. Reconciling the two investigations is the coordinator's job after both reports come back.

This is incorrect. A standard non-fork subagent starts with a fresh context window. It does not inherit the parent's conversation history or tool results. Any customer IDs, order numbers, or dispute details the subagent needs must be included explicitly in the prompt that the coordinator sends when it starts the subagent.

This is correct. In the hub-and-spoke pattern, the coordinator is responsible for error handling. A failed subagent reports back to the coordinator. The coordinator then decides whether to retry, delegate differently, or continue with what the other subagent produced. This keeps one failure from stopping the whole workflow without anyone noticing.

This is correct. A subagent runs in its own conversation, so the long tool activity it generates never builds up in the coordinator's context. The coordinator receives only the final message. This context isolation is one of the main documented benefits of delegating to subagents.
prompt.explanation:
The hub-and-spoke pattern in the Claude Agent SDK depends on two structural facts. First, every subagent is a separate agent instance with its own context window. It sees its own system prompt and the task prompt the coordinator sends, and nothing more. Its intermediate tool calls and raw results stay inside that isolated context, and the parent receives only the subagent's final report. This is a deliberate tradeoff. The coordinator cannot see the subagent's step-by-step work. In return, the coordinator's own context stays clean enough to manage several investigations at once. This matters for a support agent that handles both a billing dispute and an order history in one case.

Second, every report comes back to the hub, so the coordinator is the natural place, and the only place, for error handling. When the billing subagent fails, the coordinator can retry with a modified prompt, give the task to a different subagent, or continue with the order subagent's results and note what is missing. No spoke can make these decisions on its own, because no spoke sees the full case.

The incorrect choices depend on mechanisms that do not exist in this design. Subagents do not inherit the parent conversation, so coordinators must restate customer identifiers and dispute facts in each delegation prompt. Subagents also cannot talk to each other. Direct messaging between peers, with a shared task list, belongs to the experimental agent teams feature. That is a different collaboration mode: it gives up the hub's central observability in exchange for decentralized coordination. Treating default subagents as if they could message peers or read the parent's history leads to information gaps in production that nobody notices.

See Subagents in the SDK for context isolation and result flow, and Agent teams for the contrasting direct-messaging model.

QUESTION: Company policy caps autonomous refunds at $200, and the team also wants the agent to generally attempt a resolution before escalating. Which two design choices correctly match each rule to the appropriate mechanism? (Select TWO.)
answers: State the $200 cap in the system prompt with strong emphasis so the model is guaranteed never to exceed it.
Use a "PostToolUse" hook to reject process_refund calls above $200 so a refund over the limit never runs.
Enforce the refund cap with a "PreToolUse" hook that denies any process_refund call over $200 before it runs.
Put the preference to attempt resolution before escalating in the system prompt, knowing it is not always followed.
feedbacks: Prompt instructions are treated as context, not as enforced configuration. Compliance therefore stays probabilistic (likely but not guaranteed), no matter how strongly the rule is worded. A financial limit with real consequences needs enforcement in code, not strong wording.

PostToolUse fires only after the tool has already executed, so by the time this hook runs, the refund has been processed. The hook can send information back to the model, but it cannot prevent the call. That is why the call must be intercepted before it executes.

A PreToolUse hook runs after the model builds the tool call but before the call is processed. Code can therefore deny a refund that breaks the policy, every time. This gives the deterministic guarantee that a financial policy requires. Instructions do not give that guarantee, because the model may occasionally ignore them.

Guidance like trying to resolve before escalating is a soft preference about behavior. For this kind of rule, flexibility is useful and it is acceptable if the agent occasionally does not follow it. Prompt instructions are the right place for this kind of rule, and hooks are kept for policies that must hold on every run.
prompt.explanation:
The main architectural difference is between deterministic enforcement (the rule is applied every time) and probabilistic compliance (the model usually follows the rule, but this is not guaranteed). Hooks are code that runs at fixed points in the agent lifecycle. Anthropic's documentation describes them as making certain actions always happen rather than relying on the LLM to choose. Prompt instructions, by contrast, are loaded as context. The docs state clearly that Claude treats CLAUDE.md and system instructions as guidance, not enforced configuration. For each rule, ask what a single violation would cost. A refund over the policy limit has direct financial consequences, so it belongs behind a PreToolUse hook. This hook runs after the model has built the tool parameters but before the call is processed. It can return a deny decision that no model reasoning can override. A preference like attempting resolution before escalating is the opposite case. You want the agent to use judgment (for example, a customer who explicitly demands a human should be escalated immediately). So the flexibility of a prompt instruction is an advantage, not a weakness.

The two incorrect choices fail on opposite sides of this line. Stronger prompt wording improves the chance of compliance but never reaches 100%. Emphasis raises a rule's priority only compared with other instructions, and any failure rate above zero is unacceptable for a financial rule. A PostToolUse hook fails because of timing: it fires after the tool has already run. It is useful for normalizing or validating results and for sending feedback to the model, but it cannot stop the refund from executing. Enforcement of tool calls must happen before execution.

See the hooks guide for the description of hooks as deterministic control, the hooks reference for event timing and decision control, and the memory documentation for why instructions are context and not enforcement.

QUESTION: The agent spends several tool calls each session discovering which refund policies, return windows, and order-status codes exist. Which TWO changes supply this reference data without requiring the agent to invoke any tool to obtain it? (Select TWO.)
answers: Expose the returns policy documents and refund eligibility rules as MCP resources the agent can read directly.
Expose the "process_refund" action as an MCP resource so the agent issues refunds by reading a resource URI.
Create a "get_reference_data" tool the agent must call first in every session to retrieve policy details.
Publish the backend order-status codes and customer record schema as a read-only MCP resource catalog.
feedbacks: Policy documents and eligibility rules are reference data that the agent reads, and MCP resources exist to expose that kind of data. When they are resources, the agent immediately has an overview of the available policy content. It does not have to discover that content through tool calls.

Resources are application-driven data meant for reading. Issuing a refund is an action that changes state, and MCP tools exist for actions. Modeling an action as a resource misuses the primitive. It also does nothing to show the agent the missing reference data.

This option still requires the agent to invoke a tool to obtain the data, and the goal rules that out. It rebuilds what resources already do as a custom action. Reference data meant for reading is what MCP resources were designed to expose, without a call that the model has to invoke.

Schemas and sets of status codes are passive, read-only context, so a resource catalog is the mechanism the protocol provides for exposing them. The agent can consult the catalog at the start, instead of probing the backend tools to work out which fields and statuses exist.
prompt.explanation:
The Model Context Protocol deliberately separates tools from resources. Tools are actions that the model invokes (like processing a refund). Resources are application-driven data meant for reading, such as documents, schemas, and knowledge-base entries. Sometimes an agent uses its early turns on exploratory calls just to learn what data exists. In that case, the missing piece is almost always a content catalog, and resources are the primitive the protocol provides for that purpose. A server advertises the resources capability. It exposes its catalog through resources/list, where each entry has a URI, a name, and descriptive metadata. It serves the actual content through resources/read. The agent therefore starts each session with a self-describing overview of the available policies and schemas. It does not have to discover them through trial-and-error tool calls.

In this scenario, both the collection of returns policy documents and the backend reference data (order-status codes, customer record schema) fit that model. They are stable, readable context that informs decisions, not actions the agent performs. Building a get_reference_data tool fails the stated goal directly. The agent must still invoke a tool every session to obtain the data. The tool also puts passive data on the action side of the boundary between tools and resources. Exposing process_refund as a resource breaks that boundary in the other direction. A refund changes state, so it belongs behind a tool that the model invokes. Reading a URI does not perform the action safely, and it does not show any of the reference data the agent is missing.

See the MCP Resources specification for the catalog and read operations, and MCP server concepts for the tools-versus-resources distinction.

QUESTION: In production, some of the agent's final replies to customers end abruptly mid-sentence. The loop runs tools while "stop_reason" is "tool_use" and presents the response as finished whenever it is any other value. What should the team change?
answers: Add a system prompt instruction telling the model to keep every customer reply concise enough to fit the output limit.
Detect truncation by checking whether the final text block ends with end punctuation, such as a period, and retry the request when it does not.
Branch on the exact stop reason, treating "end_turn" as complete and handling "max_tokens" as a truncated reply.
Lower the sampling temperature so the model produces shorter and more predictable responses.
feedbacks: Prompt instructions give only probabilistic compliance (likely but not guaranteed), so some replies will still exceed the limit and arrive truncated. More importantly, the loop would still classify those truncated responses as complete, because it never checks the actual stop reason.

Parsing the response text for signs of completion is a documented anti-pattern. Complete replies can correctly end without terminal punctuation, and truncated replies can end with it. The API already provides an explicit structured signal, the "max_tokens" stop reason, so rules that guess from the text are unnecessary.

The API separates natural completion ("end_turn") from reaching the output token limit ("max_tokens"). If the loop treats every value other than tool_use the same way, truncated responses are delivered as if they were finished, and that is the bug the team observed. Checking the specific value lets the loop raise the limit or recover in another way, instead of presenting text that was cut off.

Temperature controls randomness in token selection, not response length, so it does not prevent replies from reaching the output token limit. It also leaves the loop's stopping logic unchanged, so truncated responses would still be presented as complete.
prompt.explanation:
Every API response has a stop_reason that states why generation stopped, and these values cannot be used in place of one another. "tool_use" means the model is waiting for a tool to execute. "end_turn" means it finished its answer naturally. "max_tokens" means the output token limit was reached and the reply is cut off in the middle. A loop written as "continue on tool_use, otherwise done" loses that last distinction without any warning. A truncated billing explanation is given to the customer as if it were the agent's complete answer, which matches the mid-sentence failures in the logs.

The agentic loop should branch on the specific stop reason, not on a simple continue-or-stop test. Continue while the value is "tool_use", and present the reply when it is "end_turn". Treat "max_tokens" as an incomplete response that needs handling before anything reaches the customer, for example by raising the output limit or asking the model to continue. The API provides this structured signal so that applications never have to guess from the text whether a reply is complete.

Each incorrect approach misses this. A conciseness instruction in the system prompt is probabilistic, and it does nothing to make the loop recognize truncation when truncation still happens. Checking for terminal punctuation is the classic anti-pattern of parsing natural language for control signals. It replaces a deterministic field with an unreliable rule that guesses from the text. Lowering temperature changes sampling randomness, not length. So it does not prevent truncation, and it does not correct the misclassification.

See Handling stop reasons for the authoritative definitions of each value and How tool use works for the standard loop based on stop_reason.

QUESTION: During testing, the harness returns the "lookup_order" output in a user message that places a brief explanatory text block before the "tool_result" block. The API rejects the request with a 400 formatting error. What should the developer change?
answers: Move the "tool_result" into an assistant message so it directly follows the "tool_use" turn.
Retry the request with backoff, since transient formatting errors typically resolve on resubmission.
Set "is_error" to true on the "tool_result" so the API tolerates the nonstandard block order.
Reorder the user message so the "tool_result" block appears before any text content.
feedbacks: Anthropic's API does not use an assistant message or a separate tool role for results. tool_result blocks must be sent in a user message. Putting the result in an assistant message copies how some other APIs work, but in this API it produces an invalid conversation structure.

A 400 formatting error is a deterministic validation failure, not a temporary fault. Sending the same malformed message structure again will fail every time, so retries cannot correct a wrong block order in the message content.

The is_error field tells Claude that the tool execution itself failed, so that Claude can reason about how to recover. It has no effect on the validation of message formatting. The ordering requirement for tool_result blocks applies whether or not the result is marked as an error.

The Messages API enforces strict ordering. In the user message that carries tool results, all tool_result blocks must appear before any text blocks. That message must also come immediately after the assistant's tool_use turn. Moving the tool_result ahead of the explanatory text meets this formatting rule and resolves the 400 error.
prompt.explanation:
The Messages API is stateless: your application owns the conversation history and sends it again on every request. When Claude requests a tool that the client executes, the assistant turn contains a tool_use block. Your harness must reply with a user message that contains a tool_result block with a matching tool_use_id. Beyond that pairing, the API enforces strict structural rules so the transcript can be parsed deterministically. The user message carrying results must come immediately after the assistant's tool_use message, with nothing in between. Inside that user message, every tool_result block must come before any text block. Breaking either rule produces a 400-style formatting error. The harness in this scenario caused that error by putting a text note first.

This design is useful to understand well. The model reads the growing message history as its only channel for tool outputs, so the API keeps the pairing between each request and its result unambiguous. Results are joined to requests by ID and tied to them by position. There is no special tool role. This often confuses engineers who come from APIs that model tool outputs as a separate message type. In this API, tool results are structured content inside an ordinary user message. The is_error flag is also often misunderstood. It gives Claude meaningful information about a failed tool execution. QUESTION: The "lookup_order" tool returns one message, "Error: request could not be processed", for timeouts, malformed order IDs, and missing orders alike. The agent retries unrecoverable failures and abandons transient ones. What change most directly fixes this?
answers: Add a system prompt rule instructing the agent to retry every failed "lookup_order" call three times before escalating.
Return errors that name the failure cause and include an "errorCategory" and "isRetryable" flag the agent can read.
Have the agent rate its own confidence after each failure and escalate to a human whenever that confidence is low.
Catch failures inside the MCP server and return an empty result marked successful so the agent is never confused by errors.
feedbacks: A retry policy that covers every failure applies one recovery strategy to failure types that need different ones. A timeout may justify a retry, but retrying a malformed order ID three times wastes turns. The agent also still cannot tell which situation it is in, because the error text is identical.

The error text in a tool result is the only signal the agent has when it decides whether to retry, correct its input, or give up. This change names the cause and attaches category and retryability metadata. That gives the agent the information each type of failure requires. Transient faults (temporary failures) get retried, and unrecoverable ones do not.

A model's rating of its own confidence is an unreliable proxy (indirect measure) for the kind of failure that occurred. The agent cannot work out the failure cause from a message that is identical for every cause. Rating confidence adds noise. It does not add the missing recovery signal.

Hiding errors as empty successes is an anti-pattern. It makes a backend outage look the same as a valid no-match result. The agent would tell customers that their order does not exist when the real problem was a temporary access failure.
prompt.explanation:
With tools that the client executes and with MCP tools, the model never sees your server's internals. When a call fails, the error text in the tool result is the only evidence the agent has for its next decision. This text is sent with is_error: true on the Messages API, or with isError: true in MCP responses. The official MCP guidance states clearly that the recovery hint belongs in that text, because the text is the only thing the model has to work with. Anthropic's own examples follow the same pattern. An error such as a missing required parameter is returned with text that names what was missing, and Claude can then retry with corrected input.

This is why a single uniform message such as "Error: request could not be processed" produces the opposite of the correct behavior in the scenario. The correct recovery depends on the class of failure. A transient fault (timeout, upstream outage) should be retried. A validation fault (malformed order ID) should be corrected and submitted again. A real no-match is not an error at all, and the agent should pass it on to the customer. When all three become one string, the difference is lost, so the agent guesses. It retries calls that can never succeed and abandons calls that could recover. Returning a message specific to the cause, with an errorCategory and an isRetryable flag, restores the signal at the point where the agent makes the decision.

Each incorrect approach misses that point. A fixed retry rule in the system prompt hard-codes one strategy for failure types that need different ones. Marking failures as successful empty results hides outages behind what looks like a valid no-match, so a failure becomes false information. Confidence self-ratings ask the model to make up for information it was never given. They are a weak proxy, not a replacement for descriptive errors.

prompt.explanation:
A resumed Claude Code session restores conversation state: earlier messages, tool calls, and tool results, as they were recorded. It does not read the project's files from disk again. QUESTION: Company policy requires that refunds above $500 be routed to "escalate_to_human" instead of executing. You are adding a "PreToolUse" hook to enforce this rule. Which hook design correctly blocks only the refund calls that break this rule?

Document the $500 limit in the "process_refund" tool description so the model declines to construct larger refund calls.
Match the hook on the "process_refund" tool name and inspect "tool_input" in the callback, denying calls where the amount exceeds $500.
Write a matcher expression that fires only when the "process_refund" call's "amount" argument is above $500, so compliant refunds skip the hook.
feedbacks: With asynchronous hook output, the agent continues immediately, so by the time the check completes, the tool call may already have executed. Async hooks are suitable for side effects like logging or metrics, not for blocking actions that break a policy.

Information in a tool description is prompt guidance, and compliance with it is probabilistic (likely but not guaranteed). A business rule with financial consequences needs enforcement in code, so that a call that breaks the rule cannot execute.

Hook matchers can target tools only by name, so the hook must fire on every process_refund call and then examine the tool input itself. When the amount exceeds $500, the hook returns a deny decision with a reason. This deterministically blocks the call that breaks the rule before it executes, and compliant refunds proceed normally.

Matchers filter by tool name, not by argument values, so a matcher cannot inspect the amount field of a tool call. Any condition on business fields like the refund amount must be evaluated inside the hook callback after the hook fires.
prompt.explanation:
Enforcing a refund limit in the Claude Agent SDK depends on two facts about how hooks work. First, a PreToolUse hook runs after Claude builds the tool parameters but before the call executes. This makes it the right point to intercept calls before execution, for a rule that must apply to every refund call. By contrast, PostToolUse fires only after the tool has already completed, and asynchronous hooks cannot block at all, so both are too late to prevent the refund. Second, hook matchers filter by tool name only. They cannot express conditions on business fields such as an amount, a customer ID, or a file path. The correct design therefore registers the hook for the process_refund tool name, and the callback itself reads the amount from tool_input. When the amount exceeds $500, the callback returns a deny decision, and its reason tells Claude to route the request through escalate_to_human. This is how the redirect in the policy actually happens: the blocked call never executes, and the reason directs the model to the escalation workflow.

Keep in mind the split between routing and logic. The matcher decides which tool calls reach your code. The callback body holds every condition that depends on argument values. A matcher that tries to encode the $500 threshold cannot be written, because the matching layer never sees argument contents. Asynchronous hook output fails for a different reason. It exists for side effects where nothing waits for a result, so the agent loop does not wait for it, and nothing it returns can block, modify, or annotate the call. Placing the limit in the tool description leaves enforcement to the model's judgment, which is probabilistic. For rules with financial consequences, the documented pattern is deterministic interception in code.

Have the agent rate its own confidence and automate only the cases it rates highly.
Break down accuracy by request category, such as billing disputes, before removing human review.
Expand the validation set with more sampled cases and confirm the 97% figure still holds overall.
feedbacks: A self-review step uses the same reasoning context that produced the original decision, so it is unlikely to catch systematic errors in a weak segment. It also does not tell the team whether the 97% figure is a safe basis for automation.

Self-rated confidence that is not calibrated is an unreliable proxy (indirect measure), because the model can be confident and wrong. This happens especially on the hard cases, where oversight matters most. Confidence scores are useful only after calibration against labeled data. Even then, they do not replace validating accuracy for each segment.

Aggregate accuracy can hide severe weaknesses in specific segments. A 97% overall rate is consistent with a much worse rate on one request category, such as billing disputes. Validating performance for each segment before automating is the documented safeguard against this kind of hidden weakness.

A larger sample makes the overall number more statistically stable, but it is still a single aggregate figure. It cannot reveal that one request category performs far worse than the others, and that is the risk the team needs to rule out.
prompt.explanation:
The main risk is that an aggregate accuracy metric averages over everything the system does. A 97% overall success rate can exist together with a much lower rate on one specific segment, for example billing disputes. A weak category that makes up a small share of traffic changes the headline number very little. If human review is removed based only on the aggregate, failures in that weak segment go unmonitored, and those failures have financial consequences.

An evaluation score is a distribution, not a single number. Anthropic's evaluation guidance stresses multidimensional assessment and test sets that match the real distribution of tasks, including edge cases. A single accuracy figure is only one input among several. Anthropic's agent evaluation research makes the same point: each task has its own success rate, and headline scores can tell a very different story from the reliability on each task. In practice, split the results by request category (and, for extraction-style outputs, by field). Confirm stable performance in every segment before reducing oversight.

The other approaches fail for different reasons. A larger validation set makes the confidence interval around the same aggregate number narrower, but it does not show what varies inside that number. The model tends to be wrongly confident on the hard cases in particular, and confidence can be acted on only after calibration against labeled data. answers: Acknowledge the frustration, then offer the refund, escalating only if the customer explicitly asks for a human.
Have the agent self-rate its confidence and call "escalate_to_human" when the rating falls below a set cutoff.
Score the message with sentiment analysis and escalate whenever the detected frustration exceeds a defined threshold.

feedbacks: Anger alone is not a reliable signal for escalation. The issue is clearly within the agent's capability, and the customer has not demanded a human. Under a well-designed support policy, the agent acknowledges the emotion and proposes a concrete resolution. It hands off to a person only when the customer actually requests one or when the case falls outside the agent's scope.

A self-reported confidence score does not replace explicit escalation criteria that have been evaluated. It routes cases based on an internal rating, not on documented triggers like an explicit request for a human or a gap in the policy. It also ignores the actual decision signal in this scenario, which is whether the customer asked for a person.

Customer sentiment is an unreliable proxy (indirect measure) for how complex a case is. An upset customer can have an issue that is very easy to solve. Routing on emotion instead of the customer's actual intent causes unnecessary escalations of cases that the agent could resolve.

Expressing frustration is not the same as requesting a human agent. Escalating every angry message about a solvable issue increases handoffs without need. It also works against the first-contact resolution target, because the agent could have resolved the duplicate charge directly.
prompt.explanation:
This skill depends on the difference between an explicit request for a human and an expression of frustration about a solvable issue. A well-designed support policy honors an explicit request immediately. It meets frustration with acknowledgment plus a concrete attempt to resolve the issue. Anthropic's guidance does not hard-code this rule into the model. Instead, it expects you to encode escalation criteria in your prompts, tool descriptions, and evaluations, so that the agent can recognize when a query needs human intervention. This customer is angry but has not asked for a person, and the duplicate charge is within the agent's scope. So the agent should show empathy and correct the charge, and escalate only if the customer then insists on human help.

The incorrect approaches share a common flaw: they use a proxy instead of the real signal. Treating strong language as an implied escalation demand, using a threshold on sentiment scores, or deciding based on the model's self-rated confidence all route cases on signals that do not match case complexity. Anthropic's ticket routing guidance specifically warns that Claude can give customer emotion priority over the underlying intent. It recommends explicit direction on when sentiment should and should not affect routing. A self-rated confidence cutoff has a related weakness. It replaces explicit, testable escalation criteria with an internal rating, while the documented approach is to define clear routing rules and measure escalation behavior with task-specific evals.

There is also a business side: unnecessary escalation is a measurable failure, not a safe default. Anthropic's customer support guidance treats deflection rate (inquiries resolved without human intervention) and escalation efficiency (escalating the right cases, and only those) as separate metrics to optimize together. An agent that hands off every frustrated customer lowers its deflection rate without improving escalation accuracy. The practical way to encode this boundary is with explicit escalation criteria in the system prompt, supported by few-shot examples that show both sides. One example is an explicit "get me a human" that escalates immediately. The other is an angry customer with a solvable case, which the agent acknowledges and resolves. QUESTION: Some source documents report two different figures for the same financial metric, each tied to a distinct methodology. The current schema stores one value, so one figure is dropped without any warning. How should the team redesign the output?
answers: Average the two figures into a single compromise value so the schema stays single-valued.
Have the model attach a confidence score to each value and output only the higher-rated figure.
Have the model select whichever figure it judges more credible and output only that value.
Output both values with their sources and stated methodologies, marked with a conflict flag.
feedbacks: Averaging invents a number that no source actually reported, and that is worse than either original figure. It also erases the differences in methodology that explain the gap. The output then cannot be verified against any document.

Self-rated confidence is a poorly calibrated proxy (indirect measure). The model can be confident and wrong, especially in the ambiguous cases where sources disagree. This approach still selects one value without reporting the choice, and it drops the conflict and its context.

If the model picks one value without saying that there was a choice, the conflict is lost, and so is the methodology context of the other source. Judgments about credibility made inside a single extraction pass are not reliable. The downstream consumer never learns that a disagreement existed.

Keeping both figures, with attribution and each source's methodology context, keeps the conflict visible as information instead of hiding it. Downstream systems or reviewers can then reconcile the figures deliberately. Differences in methodology often explain why credible sources disagree.
prompt.explanation:
When credible sources disagree, the disagreement itself is data. The reliable extraction pattern is to make conflicts part of the structure of the output. The schema should allow multiple values for a disputed field. Each value carries its source attribution and the source's own methodological characterization (how the source describes its method), plus an explicit conflict indicator. A government survey and an industry report can both be accurate while they measure different populations or time periods. A downstream consumer or human reviewer can reconcile them correctly only if the output keeps how each source described its own figure.

The three incorrect approaches all resolve the conflict in some way without reporting it. Picking the "more credible" value, or the value with the higher self-rated confidence, hides the conflict. It also depends on judgments that a single model pass cannot make reliably. Anthropic's guardrail guidance stresses grounding outputs in what sources actually say and checking claims against cited passages, instead of trusting the model's own assessment of correctness (see Reduce hallucinations). Averaging is the worst of the three, because it outputs a value that appears in no document at all. This breaks any ability to trace the output back to a source.

This matches Anthropic's broader guidance for work with multiple sources. Verify information across sources, track where each claim came from, and keep well-supported findings separate from disputed ones instead of combining them too early. You can wrap each document with source metadata and ask Claude to work from quoted passages. This makes the attribution easy to keep through the whole pipeline, as described in Claude prompting best practices. The design principle is that an extraction system's job is to report what the documents say, including when they disagree. Reconciliation is a separate, deliberate step with its own context. It should not be hidden inside a schema that has room for only one answer.

QUESTION: The extraction schema already captures "line_items", "stated_total", "calculated_total", and "conflict_detected". The downstream billing integration requires that "calculated_total" actually equal the sum of the line item amounts. Where should this consistency rule be enforced?
answers: Enable strict tool use so the API checks extracted values against the schema during generation.
Add a system prompt instruction telling the model to verify its arithmetic carefully before producing output.
Express the equality as a numeric constraint in the JSON schema so conforming output is guaranteed correct.
Compute the sum in application code after parsing and retry with the specific validation error on mismatch.
feedbacks: Strict tool use validates tool names and the structure of tool input parameters. It does not validate the semantic relationships between values (whether the values make sense together). It solves a different problem from the correctness of the final response, and it cannot confirm that a total matches the sum of the line items.

Prompt instructions improve the chances, but they give only probabilistic compliance (likely but not guaranteed), and that is not enforcement. When a downstream system requires the rule to hold, a deterministic check in code is needed to catch the cases that the model still gets wrong.

JSON Schema cannot express a rule across fields, such as one value being equal to the sum of an array. Even documented numeric constraints such as minimum and multipleOf are not supported for structured outputs. Conforming to the schema ensures valid JSON with the correct types, but it cannot make the arithmetic correct.

Schema conformance guarantees structure and types, not semantic correctness (whether the values are actually right). So arithmetic consistency must be checked in code after the response is parsed. Sending the specific discrepancy back with the original document lets the model correct itself. This is the documented validation-retry pattern for this type of error.
prompt.explanation:
This question tests the difference between syntactic guarantees (the output has the right form) and semantic correctness (the values in it are right). Structured outputs limit Claude's response to a schema, which guarantees valid JSON, required fields, and correct types. They do not and cannot guarantee that the numbers inside those fields agree with each other. A rule like calculated_total must equal the sum of line_items is an arithmetic relationship across fields, and JSON Schema has no way to express it. So the only reliable place to enforce it is application validation code that runs after parsing.

This is why the schema in the scenario has both stated_total and calculated_total with a conflict_detected flag. The pair exists so that downstream code can compare the values and act on discrepancies. When the comparison fails, the effective pattern is a validation-retry loop. Send the original document back together with the incorrect extraction and a specific error message, such as the computed sum compared with the stated value. Specific error feedback usually resolves arithmetic and structural mistakes in one or two retries, because the model can recheck its work against a precise complaint instead of a vague one.

The schema-constraint idea fails for a second reason. Anthropic documents numeric constraints like minimum, maximum, and multipleOf as unsupported for structured outputs, so you cannot rely on them for enforcement by the model. With raw JSON schemas, unsupported features may be rejected with a 400 error. SDK helpers may instead remove such constraints from the schema sent to the model, move them into field descriptions, and validate them on the client side. In both cases, the enforcement ends up in code, not in generation. Prompt instructions to double-check arithmetic are useful to include, but they remain probabilistic. Strict tool use concerns how Claude calls functions: it validates the structure of tool input, not the truth of extracted values.

See Structured outputs for the supported schema features and the boundary between format guarantees and semantic validation, and Strict tool use for what strict validation does and does not cover.

QUESTION: Each week, the team must extract data from a batch of documents from a 40,000-document archive, and the results are due to a downstream compliance system every Friday at 9 AM. They want the 50% discount from the Message Batches API. How should they schedule batch submissions to meet the deadline reliably?
answers: Rely on batches typically completing within one hour and submit each one shortly before the deadline.
Move the archive processing to synchronous API calls so every document completes before the deadline.
Submit each batch at least 24 hours before the results deadline to cover the maximum processing window.
Split the archive into many small batches so each individual batch is guaranteed to finish faster.
feedbacks: Most batches do complete in under an hour, but this is not guaranteed, and processing may take up to 24 hours. A plan for a hard deadline that is based on the typical completion time, and not the worst case, risks missing the compliance delivery whenever a batch runs long.

A large archive backfill with a weekly deadline is the kind of workload the batch API is designed for: nothing waits on it, and it can accept delay. Switching to synchronous calls gives up the 50% savings to solve a scheduling problem that submission timing already solves.

The Message Batches API has no latency SLA. Processing can take up to 24 hours, and a batch that has not completed by then expires. Submitting no later than 24 hours before the Friday 9 AM deadline plans for that maximum window. Submitting even earlier leaves extra time to detect and resubmit any errored or expired requests. This way the backfill, which can accept delay, gets the 50% savings and still meets the deadline.

Smaller batches are not guaranteed to finish faster. Every batch, whatever its size, has the same 24-hour processing window and no latency SLA. Splitting the workload mainly makes it easier to manage. The extra work of submitting and tracking more batches does not make the deadline any safer.
prompt.explanation:
The Message Batches API accepts higher latency in return for lower cost. It processes Messages API requests asynchronously at a 50% discount. Results are available only after all requests complete or after the 24-hour processing window expires. There is no latency SLA. Anthropic notes that most batches finish in under an hour, but nothing guarantees it, and a batch that has not completed within 24 hours expires. Plan for the full 24-hour window as the worst case. Also monitor the result of each request for errored or expired states, instead of assuming that every request will succeed.

With this approach, deadline planning becomes simple arithmetic. If results must be delivered by a fixed time, submit the first batch no later than that time minus the full 24-hour window. Submit even earlier if the team wants extra time to resubmit any errored or expired requests by their "custom_id" and receive those results before the deadline. A weekly compliance backfill is an ideal batch workload because it can accept delay. So the correct choice is to keep the discount and include the worst case in the schedule, instead of hoping for the typical case.

Each incorrect approach misunderstands the behavior. Depending on the typical completion time of under one hour treats an observed average as a commitment. This fails when a long-running batch meets a hard deadline. Going back to synchronous calls pays double for a workload that does not need low latency. Synchronous processing is meant for blocking flows, where someone is waiting. Splitting into many small batches does not help either. Smaller batches have no completion guarantee, and the 24-hour window applies to every batch. Splitting adds extra work for polling and for matching results to requests, and it does not change the worst case that the schedule must allow for.

See Batch processing for the processing window, expiration behavior, and polling model.

QUESTION: The extraction schema includes a per-value confidence score the model fills in. An audit finds several fabricated values that carried confidence scores above 0.9, so routing by the confidence field alone misses them. Which verification approach most effectively catches these fabrications?
answers: Strengthen the extraction prompt to instruct the model to report only values it is completely certain appear in the document.
Add a verification pass that locates a supporting quote in the source document for each value and flags values without one.
Raise the downstream acceptance threshold so only values with self-reported confidence above 0.98 are passed to downstream systems.
Run each extraction twice with the same prompt and accept only values on which both runs agree.
feedbacks: Instructions about certainty are vague, and the model interprets them inconsistently. Wording that asks the model to be cautious tends to reduce coverage instead of removing fabrication. A model that fabricated a value with high confidence will not reliably hold that value back just because the prompt demands certainty.

Requiring a supporting quote ties each extracted value to evidence from the source document. This directly exposes fabricated values, whatever confidence score is attached to them. This evidence-checking step is the documented pattern for verifying claims after generation. It adds to self-reported confidence instead of relying on it.

Self-reported confidence is a field that the model generates, not a calibrated probability, and the audit already shows fabricated values arriving with high confidence scores. Raising the threshold filters on the same signal that failed, so fabrications above the new cutoff still get through.

Agreement between runs filters out random variation but not systematic fabrication, because the model can produce the same believable invented value both times. This approach also doubles cost, and it never checks the value against the source document, which is where the evidence actually is.
prompt.explanation:
A self-reported confidence score is a model-produced field in your output schema. It is not a calibrated probability computed by the API. It is useful for routing: low-confidence values can go to human review, while high-confidence values continue through the pipeline. But its limits matter just as much. A fabricated value can arrive with a score of 0.95, because the number is itself generated text. When an audit shows that failure, the verification pass must check something that the confidence field cannot provide: evidence.

Anthropic's documented approach to verifying claims is to ask the model, after extraction, to find a supporting quote in the source document for each value, and to flag or retract values it cannot support. This works because grounding each value in a literal passage turns a self-assessment that cannot be verified into something that can be checked. Your code (or a reviewer) can confirm that the quote exists and actually contains the value. Confidence scores and quote verification are layers that work together: confidence decides how the review work is routed, and quotes catch the fabrications.

The other approaches fail for predictable reasons. A stricter confidence threshold filters on a signal that has already been shown to be unreliable. Prompting for certainty is a vague instruction. It reduces coverage in unpredictable ways, and it does not fix the model's inability to tell its own fabrications apart from real extractions. Running the extraction twice catches random noise but not systematic hallucination, because a believable invented value is likely to appear again. It also never consults the source document at all.

See Reduce hallucinations for the quote-grounding verification pattern and Structured outputs for why schema enforcement guarantees shape, not factual correctness.

QUESTION: Mid-session, the main agent establishes normalization rules for date and currency fields, then spawns a subagent to extract data from a batch of edge-case documents. The subagent's structured output ignores those rules entirely. What change fixes this?
answers: Pass the normalization rules explicitly in the delegation prompt sent to the subagent.
Move the normalization rules into the main agent's system prompt so subagents inherit them.
Instruct the subagent to consult the earlier conversation turns where the rules were defined.
Retry the subagent call until its output conforms to the established normalization rules.
feedbacks: Non-fork subagents start with a fresh, isolated context and receive only the prompt string passed at delegation. Any decisions, rules, or file paths the subagent needs must be stated directly in that prompt. So the fix is to include the normalization rules there.

Subagents do not inherit the parent agent's system prompt or conversation state. Each one runs with its own instructions and an isolated context. Strengthening the main agent's prompt changes nothing about what the subagent sees.

A subagent has no access to the parent conversation history, so there are no earlier turns for it to consult. This instruction would ask the subagent to use content that does not exist in its context.

Retries cannot succeed when the subagent was never given the required information. Each retry would start another subagent with a fresh context that also does not know the rules. This wastes tokens without improving compliance.
prompt.explanation:
A non-fork subagent is a separate agent instance with a fresh, isolated context. It does not receive the parent's conversation history, the parent's system prompt, earlier tool results, or files the parent already read. The only thing that passes into the subagent is the prompt string given when the task is delegated. This isolation is deliberate. It lets a subagent explore many documents and produce long output without that content building up in the main conversation. It is also the reason the delegation prompt must be self-contained. If the main agent set normalization rules earlier in the session, those rules exist only in the main agent's context. Unless they appear in the delegation prompt, the subagent behaves as if they were never written.

The other approaches all misunderstand where the boundary is. Telling the subagent to consult earlier conversation turns assumes a shared history, and isolation explicitly removes that history. Moving rules into the main agent's system prompt still leaves them on the wrong side of the boundary, because subagents run with their own instructions instead of inheriting the parent's. Retrying the call repeats the same launch with a fresh context, and it cannot produce information that was never sent. Retries help with transient (temporary) errors or format errors, not with missing inputs. The one documented exception to this isolation is a forked subagent, which copies the conversation so far. Ordinary delegation requires explicit context passing: findings and decisions must be included explicitly in every delegation.

QUESTION: Reviewer capacity is limited, so only a subset of extractions can receive human review before results flow to downstream systems. Which TWO routing approaches best target review at the extractions most likely to contain errors? (Select TWO.)
answers: Use per-field confidence scores for routing only after tests on labeled data show they predict errors.
Route extractions from ambiguous or poorly structured source documents to human review.
Ask the model to rate its own overall confidence and auto-approve extractions rated above a fixed cutoff.
Analyze the emotional tone of each incoming document's language and route strongly negative documents to review.
feedbacks: Confidence generated by the model is only text until it is checked against real results. Routing on per-field scores is valid only when evaluation against a labeled validation set shows that the scores actually separate correct extractions from wrong ones. Then the thresholds are based on measured behavior instead of the model's unverified self-assessment.

Document ambiguity is a direct, observable cause of extraction difficulty. Errors are concentrated in unclear layouts, missing fields, and inconsistent formats. Routing on this explicit criterion sends reviewer capacity to the cases most likely to be wrong.

A self-rating that is not calibrated is generated text, not a measured probability. Models are often confident and wrong on the hardest cases in particular. Without validation against labeled data, a fixed cutoff on self-ratings sends the wrong extractions to humans.

Emotional tone does not match extraction difficulty. Extracting data from a complaint letter can be very easy, while a neutral financial statement with several tables can be hard. Anthropic's routing guidance warns that giving emotion priority over intent is a failure mode, not a signal of reliability.
prompt.explanation:
This question tests the difference between explicit, validated routing criteria and unreliable proxies (indirect measures) for case difficulty. Two proxies fail in predictable ways. The first is sentiment. The emotional tone of a document says nothing about how hard it is to extract data from it. Anthropic's routing guidance explicitly documents the emotion-over-intent failure mode, where a model gives priority to a customer's expressed feelings instead of the actual information need. The guidance recommends routing on explicit factors like intent and required expertise, not tone. The second proxy is self-reported confidence. When you ask the model to rate itself, that number is only generated text, not a probability provided by the API (the Messages API response has no confidence field). Models are often confident and wrong on the hardest inputs, and that is where human review matters most.

The reliable pattern adds measurement on top of model output. Per-field confidence scores cannot be trusted by default. They deserve a role in routing only when evaluation against a labeled validation set shows that they actually predict extraction errors for this specific task. At that point, thresholds can be set where the scores clearly separate good extractions from bad ones. This matches Anthropic's broader evaluation guidance, which bases production decisions on measured accuracy against expected outcomes, not on the model's self-report. Routing on source-document ambiguity works for a related reason. It is an explicit, observable property that correlates with where extraction errors actually occur, so limited reviewer capacity goes where it adds the most value.

Anything the model claims about its own reliability must itself be validated before it drives an automated decision. Signals checked against measured data (validated thresholds, error rates by document type) can be trusted. Signals that the model invents about itself (unvalidated confidence ratings), or that only correlate with mood (sentiment), cannot. See the Ticket Routing guide and evaluation guidance for the documented approaches based on criteria and on measurement.

QUESTION: The first full batch run extracts data from 12,000 vendor contracts, but 9% of the results fail JSON schema and business-rule validation, with failures concentrated in contracts that use tabular layouts instead of narrative text. What is the most cost-effective way to resolve this?
answers: Move the failed contracts to individual synchronous API calls processed one at a time with the same prompt.
Improve the prompt using a sample of the failing contracts, then resubmit only those requests, identified by "custom_id".
Resubmit the entire 12,000-contract batch with an added instruction telling the model to follow the schema more carefully.
Configure an automatic retry loop that re-runs each failed extraction with the same unchanged prompt up to three times.
feedbacks: Switching to synchronous calls changes how the requests are delivered, not the prompt, so the failures caused by the layout continue. It also gives up the 50% batch discount on the documents that already need reprocessing.

Failures that are grouped in one layout show a systematic gap in the prompt. So the prompt should first be improved and validated on a sample of the problem documents. Batch results carry a unique custom_id for each request, so only the failed documents need to be resubmitted. This avoids paying again for the 91% that already succeeded.

Resubmitting every document reprocesses the 91% of extractions that already passed validation, and this wastes money. A vague request to follow the schema more carefully also does not address the specific tabular-layout pattern that causes the failures.

Retries with an unchanged prompt help with temporary or random formatting mistakes. They do not help with systematic failures tied to a document layout that the prompt does not handle. The same tabular contracts will keep failing for the same reason on every retry.
prompt.explanation:
The failure pattern is the main diagnostic signal. The validation errors are not random: they are concentrated in contracts with tabular layouts. This points to a systematic gap in the prompt (it was probably refined against narrative documents), not to random noise. The efficient workflow is to treat the failing documents as a new refinement sample. Improve the prompt step by step against a small number of tabular contracts, and confirm that the extractions now pass validation. Only then reprocess at scale. Anthropic recommends this same sample-first practice before any large batch, and in this case it is applied to a correction in the middle of the work. Its batch processing guidance even advises a dry run of a single request shape before you submit a batch.

The custom_id field is what makes the correction cheap. Batch results are returned as JSONL lines that may arrive out of order, so every request carries a unique custom_id for matching results to requests. The same identifier lets you find which documents failed and build a resubmission batch that contains only those. You do not pay to reprocess the 91% that already succeeded. A batch is not an all-or-nothing unit. It is a set of requests that are each matched separately, and recovery should be limited to the failing subset.

Each of the other approaches misses one half of the fix. Resubmitting all 12,000 contracts with a vaguer instruction wastes money on successful extractions, and it relies on emphasis instead of concrete criteria. Retries with an unchanged prompt and no diagnosis can recover occasional formatting mistakes. But they will fail again, every time, on documents whose structure the prompt cannot parse. Moving failures to synchronous calls changes latency and price, not the prompt, so the underlying extraction errors remain. These reviews approve nearly every extraction, yet downstream schema and business-rule validation keeps finding values in the wrong fields. What change most effectively improves review quality?

Strengthen the same-session prompt with an explicit instruction to double-check every field before approving.
Switch the review to a model with a larger context window so it can re-read the full document.
Ask the model to report a confidence score for each field and accept only high-confidence reviews.
feedbacks: An independent instance reviews the extraction without the reasoning that produced it, so it is not inclined to confirm earlier decisions. This review with a fresh view is far more likely to catch values put in the wrong field than a self-check in the same session.

A double-check in the same session still has the model's original reasoning in context, so it tends to confirm again the decisions it already made. The fact that almost every extraction is approved shows that this review path is biased by its structure. Stronger wording does not remove that bias.

The reviews fail because the reviewer shares the generator's reasoning context, not because the context is too small. A larger window still contains the same earlier reasoning, so the confirmation bias remains.

Self-rated confidence from the same session has the same bias as the review itself. A model that has just justified a wrong value to itself will also rate that value as confident. This approach filters on a poorly calibrated signal instead of adding independent judgment.
prompt.explanation:
The failure pattern (reviews that approve nearly everything while real errors get through) is the typical sign of self-review bias in the same session. When the same conversation that generated an extraction is asked to check it, the conversation history still contains the output it produced. It also contains the reasoning and the decisions it committed to along the way. Depending on the model and feature configuration, earlier thinking blocks may also remain in context. The model has already decided that a value belongs in a field. So it is much less likely to question that decision than a reviewer who sees the output for the first time. This is why Anthropic's evaluation guidance recommends a separate evaluation call. It also notes that it is generally best practice to use a different model to judge output than the model that produced it.

The architectural fix is context isolation. Give a second Claude instance only the source document and the extraction, with none of the generator's reasoning. That reviewer must work out again, independently, where each value came from, and this is the check that catches values put in the wrong field. None of the incorrect approaches breaks the shared context. Stronger double-check wording still runs inside the biased session. A larger context window changes capacity, not independence. Self-reported confidence scores are themselves produced by the reasoning being audited, so they correlate with the errors instead of exposing them.

Same-session review is similar to an author proofreading their own essay immediately after writing it, while an independent instance is similar to peer review. More thinking in the same session still happens on top of the original reasoning context, so the model is thinking again about conclusions it has already committed to. An independent review without the generator's context catches subtle issues more effectively than longer thinking by the same instance.

The problem is in the structure, not in the model's motivation. The resumed session still contains the full reasoning that produced the extraction, so the model stays tied to the conclusions it already reached. Stronger wording cannot remove the generation context that biases the review.

An independent instance has no memory of the reasoning that produced the extraction, so it judges the output on its own merits against the source document. prompt.explanation:
The failure is the documented self-review limitation: a model that keeps the reasoning context from generation is much less likely to challenge its own decisions. By resuming the extraction session, the team gave the verifier the entire conversation that produced the extraction, including the chain of reasoning that justified each value. A reviewer that already "believes" the extraction is correct will approve it without real checking. That is why approvals stayed high while errors got through.

The fix is independence in the structure of the review, not stronger prompting. Run verification in a separate instance that receives only the source document and the extracted JSON. This completely removes the tie to the earlier conclusions. The reviewer must work out again what the document says and compare it with the output. Human peer review works better than self-review for the same reason. In Claude Code and the Agent SDK, a standard subagent gives this isolation, because it starts with a fresh context window and sees nothing from the parent conversation. By contrast, a resumed session keeps its full history, including earlier tool calls, results, and reasoning. So resuming is the wrong mechanism whenever independence is the goal.

A batch cannot be modified after it is submitted. If changes are needed, the batch must be canceled and a new one created. There is no way to add tool results to a batch request that is already being processed, so this design cannot work.

Extractions that need only a single request fit the batch model well, because each batch item is an independent Messages API request. Results can arrive out of order, so the documented way to match results to inputs is the custom_id field attached to each request.

The Message Batches API processes each item as an independent Messages request, and your code does not take part while the item is processed. So there is no point where your code can intercept a tool call, execute it, and let generation continue in that same batch item. For this reason, workflows that depend on your application supplying tool results during the conversation must stay synchronous. Extractions that need only one request are ideal for batches. Server tools that Anthropic runs do execute during batch processing. So the accurate statement is that batches cannot host your application's tool loop, not that batches reject tools completely.

QUESTION: The pipeline's document-fetch tool returns the same generic "document unavailable" error whether a file is corrupted, the storage backend times out, or the document ID is invalid. The agent now retries unrecoverable failures and abandons transient ones. What change best enables correct recovery decisions?
