Instruct the agent in the system prompt to retry every unavailable document twice before skipping it.
Add automatic exponential backoff retries inside the tool for every failure before reporting unavailability.
Return structured errors that include the failure category and whether the failure is retryable.
feedbacks: Marking a failure as a successful empty result is silent suppression (hiding the failure without telling anyone), a documented anti-pattern. Downstream systems would treat missing data as a valid finding. This hides real failures and corrupts accuracy metrics instead of making recovery possible.

A fixed retry policy applied to an error that does not say what failed wastes attempts on corrupted files and invalid IDs that can never succeed. At the same time, two retries may not be enough for transient timeouts. The root problem is that the error contains no information that tells the failures apart, and no prompt rule can recover information that the tool never provided.

Internal backoff is appropriate only for transient (temporary) failures. Applying it to corrupted files and invalid document IDs adds latency with no chance of success. Even after the retries, the tool would still report the same generic status, so the agent still cannot make an informed decision.

A structured error separates transient timeouts from unrecoverable causes like corrupted files or invalid IDs. This gives the agent the information it needs to choose the right action for each case. Retry decisions become correct because the error itself carries the context, so the agent no longer has to guess from the same generic label.
prompt.explanation:
This failure is an information problem, not a retry problem. Error responses are part of a tool's interface. When a tool turns every failure mode into one generic label, the model that reads that result has no basis for choosing between retrying, correcting its input, skipping the item, or escalating. The documented pattern is to separate error categories, because each category needs a different recovery action. Transient errors (timeouts, service unavailability) need a retry. Validation errors (an invalid document ID) need a corrected input. Unrecoverable conditions (a corrupted file) need skipping or escalation, with the gap recorded.

Anthropic's tool-use guidance makes this concrete. A failed client tool call is returned as a tool_result with is_error set to true. The content should contain the specific error message, so that Claude can use it and correct itself, retrying with corrected parameters when the problem can be corrected. The same principle appears in the built-in web search tool. It returns separate documented error codes instead of one unclear status, and it separates a real error from a successful query that found nothing. An extraction pipeline should copy that design. The error payload itself should answer the question "what failed, and is a retry useful?"

A prompt rule to retry every failure twice applies one policy to failures that mean different things, because the agent still cannot tell them apart. Returning an empty result marked as success is silent suppression. Downstream consumers read the absence of data as a real finding, which is worse than an honest failure. Backoff inside the tool for every failure delays unrecoverable errors, and it does not change the generic status that caused the wrong behavior.

QUESTION: The team's extraction prompt tells Claude to "flag any document with low data quality" so flagged documents go to human review. Reviewers report inconsistent routing: clean invoices get flagged while clearly unreadable documents are not flagged. What change most improves routing consistency?
answers: Reword the instruction to stress that only genuinely problematic documents should be flagged for review.
Define concrete flag conditions, such as totals that do not add up or missing required identifier fields.
Run the extraction twice on each document and flag only documents both runs mark as low quality.
Have the model output a confidence score for each document and route those below a threshold.
feedbacks: Stronger wording still leaves the judgment subjective. On each run, the model must interpret what counts as "genuinely problematic". Making a vague instruction stronger adds no concrete content that the model can act on, so the inconsistency remains.

Replacing the subjective phrase with explicit conditions that can be checked gives the model a decision rule it can apply. A criterion like a stated total that does not match the computed total can be applied the same way on every document, and this is what produces consistent routing.

Requiring two runs to agree reduces random differences between runs. But it leaves the underlying judgment undefined, so systematic misclassifications repeat in both runs. It also doubles cost, and clearly unreadable documents that are flagged inconsistently can still get through.

Self-rated confidence is poorly calibrated, so a threshold on it only replaces one judgment that has no fixed basis with another. Without defined criteria for what makes a document problematic, the scores themselves will vary as much as the flags do now.
prompt.explanation:
This failure is a classic case of a vague instruction doing the work that explicit criteria should do. A phrase like "low data quality" has no fixed meaning. The model must invent an interpretation each time it reads a document, and nothing keeps those interpretations consistent with each other. The result is the observed symptom: flags that do not follow any stable property of the documents. Anthropic's prompting guidance is direct about this. Claude responds best to clear, specific instructions. If a colleague who received only a short briefing would be confused by the prompt, Claude probably will be too.

The fix is to turn the routing decision into a rule that the model can apply mechanically. Conditions such as "the stated total does not equal the sum of the line items" or "a required identifier field is absent from the document" can be tested against the document itself. So every run evaluates the same checks and reaches the same answer. This matches how Anthropic describes success criteria in general: "accurate sentiment classification" can be acted on, while "good performance" cannot, because only the first can be measured and enforced.

The other approaches all leave the main judgment without a fixed basis. Stressing that flags are only for "genuinely problematic" documents just repeats the vague standard more strongly. Routing on a self-reported confidence score hides the same subjective judgment behind a number. The model's stated confidence is not calibrated against any defined idea of quality. Running the extraction twice and requiring agreement is a fix for consistency, not for the criteria. Both runs share the same undefined standard, so errors that the runs have in common survive the vote, and the pipeline pays double for it.

QUESTION: A team replaces its plain-text "respond with JSON" prompt with an extraction tool whose "input_schema" is the target JSON schema, setting "strict" to true on the tool definition and parsing results from the tool call. Which TWO statements accurately describe the reliability this change provides? (Select TWO.)

Semantic checks, such as verifying line items sum to the stated total, still need code-side validation.
Syntax-level failures such as malformed JSON and missing required fields are eliminated.
Schema conformance also ensures each extracted value is placed in the semantically correct field.
feedbacks: Prompt instructions improve the chance of valid JSON, but they remain probabilistic (likely but not guaranteed). The model can still output markdown fences, extra comments after the JSON, or malformed syntax. Only output enforced by a schema gives a structural guarantee instead of a request.

Schema enforcement controls structure, not meaning. A response can be fully valid against the schema and still contain values in the wrong fields or totals that do not agree. So business-rule validation must stay in application code.

With strict tool use enabled, constrained decoding guarantees that the tool input conforms to the schema. The extraction arrives as schema-valid tool input, not as free-form text that happens to contain JSON. This removes parse failures, missing required fields, and type mismatches, which are common problems with free-text JSON responses.

This overstates what schema enforcement provides. The schema guarantees that fields exist with the right types, but the model can still put a shipping cost in a tax field or swap two values. Only semantic validation logic (checks on meaning) catches such errors.
prompt.explanation:
There are two layers of errors. Syntax errors are JSON that cannot be parsed, missing required fields, and wrong types. Semantic errors are values in the wrong fields, line items that do not add up to the stated total, and dates that contradict each other. You can define the extraction as a tool whose input_schema is your JSON schema, with strict: true set on the tool definition. This handles the first layer. Strict tool use applies constrained decoding, so the extraction arrives as a structured tool_use block whose input is guaranteed to match the schema. JSON.parse() failures and missing required fields disappear from the pipeline. Without strict mode, the documentation warns that tool calls can still leave out required fields or use incompatible types. That is why the hard guarantee comes specifically from strict: true (or, for the final response, from JSON outputs through output_config.format).

No schema can verify meaning. A schema can say that a field named total must be a number. It cannot say that the number must equal the sum of the line items. That is why production extraction systems keep a validation layer in code. For example, they extract both a calculated_total and a stated_total and flag discrepancies. They also send concrete validation errors back to the model in a retry loop. This division of work is deliberate. Schemas handle shape cheaply and deterministically, while business rules are kept in code, where they can be tested and changed over time.

Each incorrect option mixes up the two layers in a different way. The claim that schema conformance makes field placement correct assumes that a structural mechanism understands meaning. The claim that prompt wording equals schema enforcement treats a probabilistic request as a guarantee, and the documentation explicitly warns against that. Raise "max_tokens" so the response has room for both the ambiguity note and the structured extraction call.
Keep the "any" tool choice and add a stronger system prompt section demanding the note be written before the tool invocation.

Strict tool use guarantees that tool names and inputs conform to the declared schema when Claude calls tools. It has no effect on whether natural-language text appears in the response, so it does not solve the problem of the missing note.

The note is missing because forced tool use prevents text before the tool call, not because the output budget is used up. A truncated response would show a max_tokens stop reason, and that is not what the scenario describes.

With "any", the assistant message is prefilled to force tool use. This means the model cannot write explanatory text before the tool call, no matter how strongly the prompt demands it. Stronger wording does not change this mechanical limit.

The tool_choice parameter does more than encourage the model to use tools. The "any" and forced "tool" settings work by prefilling the assistant message, so the response begins directly with a tool_use block. This mechanism is what guarantees the tool call. But it also means that the structure of the response does not allow the model to write natural-language text first, even when the prompt asks for it. This is a deliberate tradeoff. You give up the ability to get explanatory text around the call, and in return you get a hard guarantee that a tool call happens.

When a workflow needs both, Anthropic's guidance is to use "auto", which lets the model produce text and then call a tool. You make the tool call reliable with an explicit instruction in the prompt. The cost is that the guarantee becomes probabilistic (likely but not enforced). This is acceptable in this case, because the team explicitly values the visible reasoning note. If the structured call were ever skipped, standard validation and retry logic would catch it downstream.

The other approaches miss the mechanism. Stronger prompt wording cannot override the prefill that "any" applies. Setting strict to true is unrelated to this problem. It enforces that tool inputs conform to the JSON schema when a call happens, not whether text comes with the call. Raising max_tokens addresses truncation. QUESTION: The system's validation step confirms extracted vendor IDs through a "lookup_reference" tool. The tool returns an empty list both when the reference service times out and when no matching record exists, so outages get logged as missing vendors. How should the tool's responses be redesigned?
answers: Add a system prompt instruction telling Claude to treat empty lookup results as potential service failures.
Have the tool mark timed-out lookups as successful empty results so downstream processing continues uninterrupted.
Have the tool set "is_error" to true on timeouts, keeping no-match lookups as successful empty results.
Retry every lookup that returns an empty result with exponential backoff until it yields matches.
feedbacks: The model cannot tell a timeout from a real no-match when both arrive as identical empty lists, so prompting cannot recover the missing signal. The difference must be carried in the tool response itself, because the model cannot infer it.

This is the silent suppression anti-pattern (hiding a failure so that nobody notices it): a failure presented as if it were a fact. The pipeline would keep recording vendors as missing whenever the reference service is down, and that is the data corruption the scenario describes.

A timeout is an access failure that needs a retry decision, while no matches is a valid, informative result of a successful query. Signaling failures explicitly through the error flag lets the caller retry outages and still correctly record vendors that are really missing.

Retrying is appropriate only for transient (temporary) access failures, not for valid empty results. Many lookups correctly have no matching record. Retrying them wastes time and tokens, and it can never produce a match that does not exist.
prompt.explanation:
The main reliability principle is that access failures (timeouts, service errors) and valid empty results (a successful query that found nothing) are outcomes with different meanings, and they need different responses. A timeout means the answer is unknown and a retry decision is needed. An empty set of matches means the answer is known: the record does not exist. When a tool returns the same empty list for both, that information is destroyed at the source. Nothing downstream, neither the model nor the pipeline, can reconstruct it. That is why the extraction system ends up logging outages as missing vendors.

The documented mechanism for signaling tool failure is the is_error flag on the tool result. It should be set to true only when tool execution actually failed. An empty tool result with a success status is a valid, documented way to say that the call worked but produced nothing. Anthropic's own web search tool follows the same convention. It returns an empty content list when a search succeeds with no matches, and a separate error object when the search itself fails. If custom tools follow the same contract, the agent and the application layer get a clear signal: retry or escalate on errors, and accept and record empty results as facts.

Each incorrect approach breaks this contract. Marking timeouts as successful empty results is silent suppression: it hides failures and corrupts the extracted data. Retrying every empty result treats valid no-match answers as failures, and it adds latency for queries that can never succeed. Prompting Claude to doubt empty results asks the model to recover a distinction that the tool response no longer contains. This is impossible, however carefully the instruction is worded.

Add a custom discovery tool that returns the full data inventory when called at the start of each run.
Paste the current inventory of collections and their structures into the coordinator's system prompt.
Expose the collection catalog and structure summaries as MCP resources the coordinator reads directly.
feedbacks: A larger budget pays for the wasted calls instead of removing them. The exploratory calls still use up turns, and their discovery output still fills the context. The goal is to make discovery unnecessary, not just affordable.

This builds a custom tool for something that MCP resources already provide as a standard primitive. Tools are meant for performing actions. Resources exist to expose readable data, such as catalogs and schemas, and clients can discover them through the standard listing mechanism.

A hard-coded inventory becomes inaccurate as soon as collections are added, removed, or restructured. The MCP server serves resources live, so the catalog that the coordinator reads always reflects the current state of the data.

MCP resources are the mechanism that the protocol provides for sharing data that gives the model context, such as file listings, schemas, and summaries. When the catalog is exposed as resources, the coordinator has a map of the available data from the start. Discovery then becomes a single read instead of a series of exploratory tool calls.
prompt.explanation:
The Model Context Protocol makes a deliberate distinction between its primitives. Tools are actions that a server performs on request (like POST endpoints). Resources are data that a server exposes for reading (like GET endpoints). The spec's own examples of resources include files, database schemas, and application-specific information. This is the same kind of inventory that this coordinator keeps discovering again on every run. When a server exposes its content catalog as resources, an agent can start each run already knowing what data exists. A long exploration over many turns becomes a single lookup.

The protocol also supplies the discovery mechanism. A server that supports resources answers the resources/list request with the set of available resources, and resources/read retrieves any of them by URI. Claude Code builds on this directly. It automatically provides tools to list and read MCP resources from connected servers, and it lets users reference them with @ mentions. For this reason, a custom inventory tool is the tempting but weaker choice. It duplicates a capability that the protocol already standardizes, and every client integration then depends on your custom tool instead of the common primitive.

The remaining options fail for more basic reasons. Hard-coding the inventory into the system prompt stores a fixed copy that goes out of date as soon as the data changes, while a live resource catalog always reflects the current state of the server. Raising the tool-call budget only pays for the wasted turns. The exploratory output still fills the coordinator's context with extra content before any real delegation happens.

Add a retry loop that regenerates the report whenever the citation format check fails.
Add the citation rules to the subagent's description field so Claude applies them during delegation.
Move the citation formatting rules into the report subagent's own system prompt in its AgentDefinition.
feedbacks: More emphasis in the coordinator's system prompt does not help, because that prompt is never part of the subagent's context. The subagent receives its own AgentDefinition system prompt, not the parent's instructions.

The description field tells the coordinator when to delegate to a subagent. It is a signal for choosing the subagent, not a set of behavioral instructions. Rules that control how the subagent works belong in its system prompt, not in its description.

When you place the citation rules in the subagent's own AgentDefinition system prompt, they are directly in the context that controls its behavior.
prompt.explanation:
In the Claude Agent SDK, each subagent is configured through an AgentDefinition. Its two required fields are description and prompt, and they have very different roles. The description is what the delegating agent reads to decide when to invoke the subagent. The prompt is the subagent's own system prompt, and it defines how the subagent behaves once it is invoked. Confusing the two is a common design error.

The more basic idea is context isolation. A non-fork subagent begins in a fresh conversation. It receives its AgentDefinition system prompt, the task prompt passed through the Agent tool, the project CLAUDE.md, and its tool definitions. It does not receive the parent's conversation history, the parent's tool results, or the parent's system prompt. This isolation is the purpose of subagents: it keeps long, detailed exploration out of the main context, and it lets each worker have specialized instructions. But it also means that any behavioral rule a subagent must follow has to be in that subagent's own definition or be passed explicitly in the delegation prompt. Rules written for the coordinator do not pass down to the subagents.

That is why strengthening the coordinator's prompt cannot work. It is also why the description field is the wrong place for behavioral rules, and why a loop that regenerates on failure only wastes tokens retrying an agent that was never given the rules. Suppose a search subagent returns a free-form narrative with URLs mentioned in different places in the text. Summaries compress, reorder, and merge sentences, and the loose link between a statement and a nearby URL is the kind of detail that gets dropped. The fix is to make the link explicit where the data is created. Each subagent emits claim-to-source mappings in which the finding, the source URL, the document name, and the date are separate fields. The synthesis agent then works on records that it must pass on intact, instead of free-form text that it is free to rewrite.

This matches Anthropic's own guidance. The prompting best practices recommend separating document content from source metadata with structured tags, instead of mixing provenance into the body text. They also recommend structured formats like JSON for state that later steps depend on. The API's search_result content blocks follow the same design. A source identifier and a title are in dedicated fields, separate from the content text, so that attribution is machine-readable and does not have to be inferred. With the Agent SDK, structured output from a subagent can be validated against a schema, which gives the coordinator a predictable payload to pass into synthesis.

Enable "multiline" so the search output includes the lines surrounding each match.
Set "output_mode" to "content" so the search returns matching lines with line numbers.

feedbacks: The count mode returns how many matches occur in each file, plus a total. It does not return the matched text. It is useful for measuring how widespread a pattern is, but it gives the agent nothing it can quote.

The multiline option changes how patterns are matched, so that a single pattern can span line boundaries. It does not change what the tool outputs, and it does not add surrounding lines to the results. So it does not solve the problem of getting the matched text.

Grep's output mode controls what the search returns, and the default mode reports only the files that contain matches. When the mode is switched to content, the same search returns the matching lines along with the file and line information. This is what the agent needs to quote the statistic.

Reading every matched file in full would eventually show the lines. But it uses many tool calls and loads entire documents into context when only a few lines are needed. Grep can return the matching lines directly, so this approach is wasteful, not efficient.
prompt.explanation:
Claude Code's Grep tool has three output modes, and choosing the right one is part of using the tool well. The default mode, files_with_matches, returns only the paths of files that contain a match. The content mode returns the matching lines themselves, together with the file and line number. The count mode returns the number of matches in each file, plus a total. The default exists to save tokens. In a large corpus, listing paths costs far less than putting every matching line into context, and often a path list is all the agent needs before it decides where to read further.

In this situation the agent's goal is the opposite. It needs the matched text word for word so it can quote it. Setting "output_mode" to "content" gets those lines in a single call. Using Read on every returned file instead would work, but it loads whole documents to get back a few lines. That is the context waste that targeted search exists to avoid. The count mode answers a different question (how common a pattern is). The "multiline" setting is a matching option that lets a pattern span line boundaries. It is not an output option that adds context lines.

Grep is not only a way to "find the files". It is a configurable search, and the level of detail in its output should match what the next step needs: path lists for navigation, line content for quoting and analysis, and counts for measuring how common a pattern is. Switch to a model with a larger context window so full findings reach synthesis without being shortened.
Strengthen the synthesis agent's system prompt with an explicit instruction to cite a source for every claim.

When findings are compressed into free-form text, the link between each claim and its source is not carried forward, and the synthesis agent can cite only what is in its input. When claim-source mappings are carried through the summary step as structured data, provenance (where each claim came from) stays intact, however much the text is compressed. On short tasks, the full findings pass through and the citations are correct. This contrast confirms that the summary step is where attribution is lost.

The lost-in-the-middle effect is about reduced attention to information that is present in a long input but placed in the middle of the context. In this scenario the summary is short, and the problem is that the source attribution is no longer in the input at all. Moving the summary to a different position cannot bring it back.

A larger context window only delays the point at which the accumulated findings must be shortened. Recall in long inputs also still gets worse as they grow. The structural fix is to make attribution survive the summary step, not to avoid summarizing until the next, larger limit is reached.

The same synthesis agent produces correct citations on short tasks with the same prompt, so weak instructions are not the problem. Even a strict instruction to cite everything cannot help when the sources were already removed from the input. The agent would have to invent attributions.
prompt.explanation:
This failure shows a core principle of synthesis from many sources: source attribution is lost during summarization unless claim-source mappings are preserved as structured data. A summary loses information. Once a figure, quote, or finding is rewritten as free-form text, the link back to the URL or document it came from is gone. No later agent, however well prompted, can recover provenance (where a claim came from) that was never given to it. Attribution must be preserved; it can never be reconstructed.

The diagnosis is based on a controlled comparison. The subagents, the synthesis agent, and its prompt are the same on short and long tasks. The only difference is the summary step that the coordinator adds on long tasks. This identifies the summarization as the point where attribution disappears. Anthropic warns about the same mechanism with compaction: after a conversation is compacted, the summary is all the model has of the earlier work, so anything the summary must keep has to be stated explicitly. The structural fix has two parts. Subagents must emit structured claim-source mappings (claim, evidence excerpt, source name or URL, publication date). The coordinator must then carry those mappings through every summary step as data, not as free-form text.

Each incorrect fix targets the wrong layer of the problem. A citation instruction in the synthesis prompt controls behavior, not the content of the input, so it fails in the same way when the sources are missing. Moving the summary to a new position addresses the lost-in-the-middle effect. That effect describes weaker attention to information that is still present in a long input, but in this case the sources are missing completely. A larger context window only delays summarizing and adds cost, and recall in long contexts still gets worse as they fill.

Constrain the tool's "input_schema" so the parameter accepts a reference from the indexed document catalog rather than any URL string.
Add a system prompt rule stating that "load_document" must only be used for document retrieval, never for general web pages.
Set "strict" to true on the tool definition so grammar-constrained sampling guarantees only approved document sources are passed.
feedbacks: Backend validation is where business rules such as source authorization are actually enforced, because a schema alone cannot know which targets are approved. Returning a validation error also gives the agent a clear signal to correct its request, instead of failing in a way that nobody notices.

A narrower input schema changes which requests can be expressed through the interface at all, so unrestricted web addresses no longer fit the tool's contract. This limits the capability through the structure of the tool, instead of asking the model to restrict itself.

Prompt instructions are probabilistic (not guaranteed) guidance, not enforcement. Under some conditions, the agent can still pass a target that is not a document. The misuse in the logs happened because nothing at the interface level prevented it, and a prompt rule does not change that.

Strict tool use guarantees that tool inputs match the declared JSON schema in structure and types. But it cannot check whether a string value points to an approved repository. Source authorization is business logic. It belongs in the schema's constraints and in the tool implementation, and strict mode alone cannot provide it.
prompt.explanation:
Replacing a generic tool with a constrained alternative works because it moves the restriction from the model's judgment into the tool's interface. Two mechanisms do this work together. First, the input_schema defines which requests can be expressed at all. If the parameter is a reference into the indexed document catalog instead of a free-form URL string, the tool's contract no longer accepts search results pages or forum threads. Second, the tool's implementation validates each request against the approved document repositories, and it returns a validation error when the target is outside them. The schema limits the shape of valid inputs, and the backend checks the business rule that the schema cannot express. This is the principle behind the documented pattern of replacing fetch_url with a document-specific tool: unwanted behavior becomes impossible, not just discouraged.

The tempting wrong choice is strict: true. Strict tool use applies grammar-constrained sampling, so that tool_use.input is guaranteed to match the tool's JSON schema. This removes inputs that are malformed or have the wrong types. But it enforces the shape and types of the schema, not authorization. A syntactically valid string that happens to be a search engine URL still passes. Strict mode adds to a well-constrained schema; it does not replace that schema or backend validation. A system prompt rule is even weaker, because it depends on probabilistic (not guaranteed) compliance. The logs in this situation already show that the agent misuses capabilities that remain available to it.

See Define tools for schema and description design, and Strict tool use for what grammar-constrained sampling does and does not guarantee.

Forcing a specific tool is meant to guarantee a particular step in a workflow, not to fix unclear tool selection. It also depends on a fragile keyword rule to decide when to force the tool. This only moves the routing problem into custom logic, instead of fixing the overlapping definitions.

Tool descriptions are the main mechanism Claude uses to select tools, and the nearly identical names and descriptions are the root cause of this misrouting. When you rename the tool and rewrite its description to cover only web search output, the overlap in meaning disappears. At selection time, it is then clear which requests belong to each tool.

prompt.explanation:
Claude decides which tool to call based on the user request and each tool's description. Anthropic describes detailed descriptions as by far the most important factor in tool performance. When two tools have nearly identical names and descriptions, the model has no reliable signal to tell them apart, so misrouting is a predictable result and not a model failure. Anthropic's troubleshooting guidance names description ambiguity as the likely cause when Claude calls the wrong tool. The documented fix is to make the tools different in when to use them, not only in what they do.

Renaming the search tool to something like process_web_results, and rewriting its description to mention only information retrieved from web searches, removes the overlap at its source. Good descriptions state what the tool does, when it should be used, and when it should not be used. A name that reflects the tool's domain (web results or local documents) makes the same boundary clearer.

The other approaches work around the ambiguity instead of removing it. Few-shot routing examples depend on probabilistic (not guaranteed) pattern matching, and they increase prompt tokens while the confusing definitions stay. A forced tool_choice exists to guarantee a specific action, such as running a particular extraction first. It also depends on already knowing which tool is correct, and that is the open question in this case. A pre-delegation classifier rebuilds the model's own selection capability as extra infrastructure. It adds a new point of failure, and the root cause is not touched.

answers: An urgency rating plus timing data on how long each subagent ran, so the analyst can prioritize the case appropriately.
The complete raw outputs from every subagent so the analyst can work directly from all of the gathered evidence themselves.
A structured summary with the findings gathered so far and their sources, what is blocking progress, and a recommended next step.
Only the research topic and a conflict category label, so the analyst forms an independent judgment without anchoring bias.
feedbacks: Urgency and runtime metadata help to prioritize the queue, but they say nothing about the case itself. The analyst still does not have the findings, the nature of the conflict, or any recommendation, so the investigation would have to start over.

Raw subagent outputs pass on a large amount of unprocessed text instead of the state of the case. The analyst would have to repeat the synthesis work that the agents already did, just to find the conflicting claims. This defeats the purpose of a handoff in the middle of the process.

The analyst cannot see any agent threads, so the handoff must be complete on its own. A structured summary passes on the findings collected so far with their attribution, explains why the work is blocked, and proposes a next action. With it, the analyst can resolve the conflict without redoing the investigation.

Holding back the completed analysis forces the analyst to investigate again from the beginning, and the work the system already did is thrown away. Avoiding anchoring bias (being influenced too much by the first information you see) does not require throwing away findings. The analyst can weigh the evidence presented and still make an independent judgment.
prompt.explanation:
An escalation in the middle of a process is a handoff of case state, and its design depends on what the receiver can and cannot see. When the human who receives it has no access to the agent threads or transcript, the handoff message is the only channel that carries the investigation's progress forward. A structured summary therefore needs three things. It needs the findings collected so far, with their source attribution. It needs a root cause analysis of why the system could not continue (in this case, two credible sources in direct conflict). And it needs a recommended action. With this package, the human can continue from the point where the agents stopped, decide how to reconcile the sources, and avoid paying again for the research already done.

Each incorrect approach breaks this transfer in a different way. Sending all the raw subagent outputs hands over evidence without analysis. The structure that made the findings usable is lost, and the analyst must redo the synthesis just to find the conflict. Sending only a topic and a category label deliberately throws away completed work. It accepts a full re-investigation that is sure to happen in order to avoid an imagined risk of anchoring (being influenced too much by the first information you see). Urgency ratings and runtime statistics are metadata for prioritizing, not case content. They tell the analyst how fast to act, but not what to act on. Anthropic's customer support guidance treats escalation as a behavior to design and measure explicitly, and the same principle applies in multi-agent architectures. Whoever receives a handoff, human or agent, knows only what the handoff message explicitly contains.

Logs show the agent retrying calls that were denied for lack of permission and abandoning simple timeouts. Which TWO changes to the tool's error response fix this recovery behavior? (Select TWO.)

Add an "isRetryable" boolean alongside a human-readable description of what actually went wrong.
Include an "errorCategory" field distinguishing transient, validation, and permission failures.
Return failures as successful results with empty content so the workflow is not interrupted.
feedbacks: A single retry rule for every case hard-codes one recovery strategy for error types that need different strategies. Retrying a permission denial twice still fails, and two retries may not be right for every transient outage. The agent needs information about each error, not one policy for all of them.

A retryability flag gives the agent a clear signal about whether another attempt can succeed. The descriptive message lets it adjust its approach or explain the failure. Together, these replace guessing with recovery decisions based on information.

An error category tells the agent which recovery path applies: retry transient failures, fix the inputs on validation failures, and escalate permission failures. This directly addresses the confusion seen in the logs between permission denials and timeouts.

Marking a failure as a success is silent error suppression (hiding errors so that nobody notices them), which is a known anti-pattern. The agent would treat an outage as a valid empty result. Gaps in coverage would then enter the final report as if the searches had really found nothing.
prompt.explanation:
An agent can recover from a tool failure only as well as the error response allows. A bare string like "Error" gives the model nothing to reason about, so it guesses, and in this case it guesses the wrong way around. It retries permission denials that will never succeed, and it gives up on timeouts that a single retry would fix. The fix is to return structured error metadata inside the tool result. This includes an errorCategory that separates transient failures (retry), validation failures (fix the input and retry), and permission failures (escalate). It also includes an isRetryable boolean and a human-readable message. These category and retryability fields are a design choice for the application's payload; they are not built-in protocol fields. The signal at the protocol level is the error flag itself, written as isError: true in MCP tool results and is_error: true in Messages API tool result blocks.

Errors belong inside the result, where the model can see them, for a reason that is central to how tool use works: the model reads the failure text and corrects itself. Anthropic documents that when a tool result has an error message and the error flag is set, Claude includes the failure in its reasoning. For input problems that can be fixed, it retries with corrected parameters. Hiding the failure stops this mechanism completely. Returning an empty result marked as a success turns an outage into false information that goes into the final cited report. A prompt rule that retries everything twice applies one recovery strategy to error types that need three different ones.

See Handle tool calls for error handling in tool results and MCP Tools specification for the distinction between protocol errors and tool execution errors reported with the error flag.

The subagent emits only the facts, supporting quotes, and relevance signals that the synthesis agent actually needs. Anthropic also advises against structured output fields that request step-by-step reasoning, because they make the output larger and can cause schema failures.

A required field that records the model's full step-by-step analysis defeats the purpose of the schema. The chain of reasoning uses most of the tokens and adds little that the synthesis step can use. Anthropic's documentation goes further. Structured output properties that request model thinking or step-by-step reasoning are an explicit anti-pattern that can even cause a refusal, and the guidance is to prefer short explanations and evidence fields instead.

Everything a subagent returns becomes input that the coordinator and the later agents must carry, and as that input grows, accuracy and recall get worse. Compressing at the source keeps the useful information on purpose. The other options in this question do not. Truncation by the coordinator cuts the field without looking at its content, after the expensive tokens were already generated. A brevity instruction in the prompt is probabilistic (not guaranteed), and it keeps the reasoning field in the schema contract. Raising max_tokens controls how long a response the synthesis agent may generate, which is unrelated to how much handoff input it must take in.

Place the "tool_result" block inside an assistant message rather than a user message in the history.

Your harness runs the tool and then appends a new user message containing a tool_result block whose tool_use_id refers back to that id. Because the assistant message with the tool request is missing, the tool_result no longer directly follows its matching tool_use, and the API rejects the request as malformed.

The API is stateless: the server does not remember anything about the earlier turn, so the conversation history you send is the only record of what Claude asked for. The pairing rules (a result must directly follow its request, matched by ID) exist so that the model can connect each piece of returned data to the call that produced it without confusion, even when several tools run in one turn.

Extend "old_string" with more surrounding lines until the match becomes unique.
Switch to Bash and modify the targeted occurrence with a sed command.
feedbacks: When the repeated structure of a file prevents Edit from finding a unique match, the documented fallback is to Read the full file, build the complete modified contents, and Write the whole file. This makes the single intended change reliably, without depending on the text being unique.
The replace_all option changes every occurrence of the target string, but only one of the 12 blocks should change. Using it in this case would corrupt the other 11 blocks, which must stay unchanged.

Adding surrounding context is the usual first fix for a match that is not unique. But the scenario states that the boilerplate repeats identically, so no amount of nearby text can tell one block from another. In this file, uniqueness cannot be achieved this way.

The Edit tool performs exact string replacement. It takes an old_string and a new_string, with no regex or fuzzy matching, and it enforces a uniqueness rule. By default, the target string must appear only once in the file. If it matches several locations, the call fails instead of guessing. This design is deliberate. Editing the first match automatically, without telling anyone, could change the wrong place, so the tool refuses until the intent is clear.

Add a system prompt rule telling the subagent to retry whenever the returned result type looks wrong.
Reuse the original "analyze_document" description across all three tools so the model sees them as related.

feedbacks: Tools built for a specific purpose are useful because they have defined contracts. Extraction returns structured data points, summarization returns free-form text, and verification returns a verdict with evidence. Responses that contain only the fields the receiving agent needs remove the parsing failures caused by mixed output, which were the reason for the split.

Retrying after a wrong result treats the symptom and depends on probabilistic (not guaranteed) compliance, instead of fixing the interface. Once each tool has a clear contract and a distinct description, the wrong result type should rarely occur at all.

Identical or nearly identical descriptions are a documented cause of misrouting, because the model cannot tell apart tools whose descriptions overlap. Reusing one description for all three tools creates again the ambiguity that the split was meant to remove.

Descriptions are the main mechanism the model uses to choose among tools, and three related tools create the risk of overlap that boundary language resolves. When each description states when that tool should be used, and when a related tool is the right choice, the new tools are not misrouted in the way the old generic tool was misused.

Splitting a generic tool helps only if the model can clearly tell the new tools apart at the two points where it works with them: selection time and result-consumption time. At selection time, the model reads the tool descriptions, which are its main basis for choosing among tools. Anthropic recommends detailed descriptions that say what a tool does, when to use it, and when not to use it. For related tools, this means explicit boundary language that points to the right alternative. At consumption time, each tool's output contract decides whether later agents can parse the results reliably. The documented guidance is to return high-signal responses that contain only the fields the task produces, so that a verification verdict never arrives mixed into a summary.

A tool is an interface specification, not a collection of every capability. The original analyze_document failed because one contract tried to carry three different result shapes, and the consumers had to guess which shape they had received. Note the opposite case, though. Resend the identical request unchanged, repeating until the model eventually returns "end_turn".
Treat the response as truncated and retry the request with a higher output token limit before using it.

Resending the same request with the same output limit will keep reaching the same limit, so the loop would never make progress. Retrying without changing anything does not address the cause of the truncation.

A "max_tokens" stop reason means that generation stopped because the output limit was reached, so the response is incomplete. The loop should handle it as a separate case, usually by raising the limit and retrying. It should not treat the response as a tool request or as a finished answer.

A response that stopped at the token limit is cut off in the middle of generation; it did not finish naturally. Passing it to the coordinator as a completed result would send truncated and possibly misleading analysis to the later stages.
prompt.explanation:
The agentic loop is based on stop_reason. This field covers every possible reason for why generation stopped; it is not a yes-or-no flag. tool_use means Claude emitted structured tool requests and expects results back. end_turn means it finished naturally and the loop can exit. But other values exist, and a reliable loop must handle them explicitly. max_tokens means the output reached the configured limit in the middle of generation. The content is truncated, and it may contain an incomplete tool call or a half-finished analysis. Nothing about the response shows that it is complete.

The correct handling is a separate path. Recognize the truncation and retry with a larger output token limit, or restructure the task so that the output fits. This matters especially in a multi-agent pipeline. A subagent that returns a truncated document analysis, without anyone noticing, damages everything after it. The synthesis and report agents will build on incomplete findings with no signal that anything was lost.

Each of the other approaches breaks the loop's contract. Treating max_tokens like end_turn turns an incomplete response into a final result. Parsing the response text for tool names brings back the classic anti-pattern of inferring control flow from natural language instead of from structured signals. Tools should run only when the response contains actual tool-use content blocks. Resending the identical request changes nothing, because the same limit produces the same truncation, so the loop repeats without progress.

Setting tool_choice to any forces a tool call, but Claude still decides which tool to call. The problem in this scenario is that Claude picks the wrong tool, so guaranteeing that a call happens does nothing to improve the selection.

The documented fix is to make the tools different in when to use them, not only in what they do.

It recommends that they cover what the tool does, when it should and should not be used, and its caveats.

Increase each subagent's context window allocation so more sources fit within the existing fixed pipeline stages.
Switch to dynamic decomposition where the coordinator spawns new subtasks based on intermediate findings.

feedbacks: The synthesis subagent can work only with findings that were actually researched, and no subagent collected material on the missed subtopics. Asking it to fill gaps from nothing tends to produce unsupported or hallucinated content, not real coverage.

The problem is not that subagents run out of room for sources. The problem is that no task was ever created for the newly discovered subtopics. A larger context does not change what the coordinator assigns.

Fixed pipelines work when all the steps are known in advance, but open-ended research reveals new areas during the task. Dynamic adaptive decomposition lets the coordinator create additional subtasks when analysis finds new subtopics, and this directly closes the coverage gaps.

Adding one more predetermined step to the pipeline keeps the decomposition fixed. If the second search pass finds even more subtopics, the same gap appears again, because the structure still cannot adapt to what is discovered.
prompt.explanation:
Anthropic's architectural guidance makes a clear distinction between two styles of decomposition. Prompt chaining (a fixed sequential pipeline) is the right choice when a task "can be easily and cleanly decomposed into fixed subtasks". Every step is known in advance, each LLM call processes the output of the previous call, and you can insert programmatic checks between steps. In the orchestrator-workers pattern, by contrast, a central agent breaks down the task dynamically, delegates to workers, and synthesizes the results. This pattern exists for tasks where the needed subtasks cannot be predicted in advance.

Open-ended research is the standard example for the dynamic approach. Suppose the document analysis subagent discovers that a topic has unexpected dimensions. A fixed search-analyze-synthesize-report sequence has no mechanism to act on that discovery, because the plan was decided before any findings existed. An adaptive coordinator uses intermediate findings as input to planning. It creates new search or analysis subtasks for each newly found subtopic until the coverage criteria are met. This choice has real costs, which is why Anthropic recommends starting with the simplest structure. Dynamic decomposition costs more tokens and latency, and its results are harder to reproduce. So predictable jobs that follow a template (a weekly brief with the same sections every time) should stay on fixed pipelines.

Each incorrect option misses the root cause. Adding another fixed step only moves the limit to a later point. The structure still cannot react to whatever the extra step finds. Prompting the synthesis subagent to infer missing subtopics cannot create research that was never done, and pushing it to do so encourages fabrication. Larger context windows address capacity, not planning. The coordinator never created tasks for the missed areas, so no amount of extra room changes what reaches the report.

Add a pipeline step that re-runs the review whenever the comment format differs from the last run.
Rewrite the formatting rules again, marking every required field as IMPORTANT.

The situation states that several rewrites of the prose (ordinary written sentences) have already failed to produce consistency. Another rewrite with stronger emphasis repeats the same approach that is not working. Emphasis raises priority only relative to the surrounding instructions. It does not show what the output should actually look like.

Self-rated confidence is about whether a finding can be trusted, not whether its format is consistent. The model can be confident in a comment that has a different structure from the last run, so filtering by confidence does not change the formatting inconsistency.

A small set of input/output examples (a raw finding next to the exact comment it should become) communicates structure, severity labeling, and tone in one place. This removes the room for interpretation that written instructions leave open.

Written rules tell Claude about the format, while examples show it. When a transformation is shown two or three times across varied cases, it makes clear the details that each rewrite of the rules still leaves open. The prompting best practices call well-made examples one of the most reliable ways to control output format and structure. answers: Pipe an empty line to stdin so the interactive session receives input and terminates cleanly.
Invoke Claude Code with the "-p" flag so it prints the result and exits without waiting for input.
Add "--output-format json" so the run emits machine-readable output and terminates when it finishes.
Raise the CI job timeout so the interactive session has enough time to complete the review.
feedbacks: Sending made-up input to the interactive UI is a fragile workaround, not the supported mechanism for automation. The documented pattern is non-interactive mode, where stdin and stdout behave like a standard Unix command-line tool.

The "-p" (or "--print") flag runs Claude Code in non-interactive mode. It processes the prompt, writes the result to stdout, and exits. This is the documented way to run Claude Code in automated pipelines, where no human is present to interact with the terminal UI.

The "--output-format" option controls how results are formatted in print mode. On its own, it does not take Claude Code out of the interactive UI. It is useful for parsing results in CI, but only after the run is already non-interactive.

The job is not slow. It is blocked, waiting for interactive input that will never arrive. A longer timeout only delays the failure and wastes runner time, because an interactive session in CI never ends on its own.
prompt.explanation:
Claude Code has two fundamentally different execution modes. By default, the claude command starts an interactive terminal session that waits for a human to type, approve actions, and direct the conversation. In a CI runner there is no human, so that session blocks until the pipeline's timeout kills it. The -p flag (long form --print) switches to non-interactive mode. Claude Code takes the prompt, does the work, prints the result to stdout, and exits with code 0 on success or a non-zero code on failure. A pipeline step needs exactly this exit-code behavior, and this is why Anthropic documents -p as the way to run Claude Code in CI, pre-commit hooks, and batch scripts.

claude -p behaves like any other Unix command-line tool. You can pipe content into it (for example, pipe a diff into a review prompt) and pipe its output to the next command. Options like --output-format json are then useful for producing machine-parseable results that a script can turn into pull request comments. But output formatting controls what is emitted, not whether the process waits for a user. In the same way, a longer timeout treats a deadlock as a performance problem. Sending fake keystrokes to the interactive UI is a fragile hack when a non-interactive mode built for this purpose exists.

QUESTION: You are defining the JSON schema that the review pipeline uses to extract findings from pull requests. Fields like the file path and severity are always determinable from the diff, but a referenced CVE identifier frequently is not. How should the schema handle these fields?

Mark every field in the schema nullable so the model is never forced to supply a value it cannot verify.
Keep all fields required and instruct Claude in the prompt to output the string "unknown" when a value is missing.
Keep the always-present fields required and make only the CVE identifier nullable, allowing a JSON null value when absent.
feedbacks: Retry with error feedback fixes format and structural errors, but it cannot create information that is not in the source. If the pull request mentions no CVE, every retry against a required, non-nullable field will again force the model to invent one.

Making every field nullable gives up the guarantee that fields always present in the source are filled in. Later consumers must then handle null file paths and severities that should never occur. Nullability should be limited to fields that are actually uncertain in the source, not applied to all fields.

A sentinel string (a special placeholder value) goes around the type system instead of using it. Later code must now recognize a special value, and nothing in the schema stops the model from producing a plausible invented identifier instead of the sentinel. Expressing absence as a JSON null value in the schema is the documented pattern that can be enforced.

The schema design should match the source data. Fields that are guaranteed to exist stay required. Fields that the source may lack are made nullable, so the model can return a JSON null value. This prevents the model from inventing a CVE identifier to satisfy a required field, and later tools can still rely on the file path and severity being present.
prompt.explanation:
The core principle is that a schema should express what the source data actually guarantees. Structured output mechanisms ensure that every required field is present in the result. That guarantee is what turns a required field into a trap that causes fabrication when the underlying document does not contain the information. If a CVE identifier is required and non-nullable but the pull request mentions no CVE, the only way for the model to produce valid output is to invent one. Anthropic's documentation warns about this directly: when required parameters cannot be based on the input, Claude may infer or guess plausible values.

The supported JSON Schema subset includes union types, such as a type array of string and null. This lets the model express absence honestly as a JSON null value (not the string "null"). It is usually combined with a prompt instruction to return null when the document gives no evidence. The judgment that the question tests is scoping: nullability belongs only on fields that the source may really lack. Making every field nullable removes the guarantee of presence that later CI tools depend on for fields like file path and severity. The docs also note that optional parameters and union types increase the complexity of the compiled grammar, so they should be used where uncertainty is real, not everywhere.

The other approaches fail for structural reasons. A sentinel string (a special placeholder value) like "unknown" moves the handling of absence out of the schema and into a convention that nothing enforces, and the model can still emit an invented identifier that parses perfectly. A validation retry loop is valuable for format and arithmetic errors. But retries cannot recover information that is not in the source, and each retry creates the same forced choice between refusing and inventing. Remember that structured outputs constrain format, not truth. Schema design and grounding instructions, not retries, keep missing data from becoming invented data.

QUESTION: The pipeline's prompt instructs Claude to "handle null values gracefully" when generating tests for migration scripts. Across runs, the generated tests inconsistently expect nulls to be skipped, defaulted, or rejected. What prompt change most effectively fixes this?
answers: Have Claude rate its confidence in each generated test and discard low-confidence ones.
Rewrite the prose instruction with stronger wording stating null handling must be consistent.
Provide two or three concrete test cases showing a null input and its expected output.
Re-run test generation several times and keep only the tests that agree across runs.
feedbacks: Self-rated confidence is unreliable, because the model can be confident and wrong, and each inconsistent interpretation may come with high confidence. Filtering by confidence does not tell Claude which null behavior the team actually expects.

Stronger wording does not resolve the underlying ambiguity, because the prompt still never says what the correct null behavior is. Claude would still be free to interpret graceful handling as skipping, defaulting, or rejecting, only with more emphasis.

Concrete input/output examples are the most effective way to communicate an expected transformation when written descriptions are interpreted inconsistently. A couple of examples that show what a null input should produce remove the ambiguity that causes different behavior across runs.
Majority voting treats the symptom, not the cause, and it adds cost to every pipeline run. If the specification is ambiguous, the runs that happen to agree may still contain the wrong null behavior.
prompt.explanation:
The failure in this question is a specification gap, not a problem with the model's reliability. An instruction like "handle null values gracefully" is subjective. Skipping the row, substituting a default, and rejecting the record are all reasonable readings of graceful handling, so each generation run can choose a different one. No amount of emphasis, retrying, or confidence filtering changes the fact that the prompt never states which behavior is correct.

The documented fix is to show the behavior instead of describing it. Anthropic's prompt engineering guidance names few-shot examples as the most effective technique for producing output that is consistently formatted and correct. It recommends making the examples varied enough to cover edge cases, so that Claude does not infer an unintended pattern. Two or three concrete pairs, such as a row with a null email that produces a record with the field omitted, define the expected transformation clearly. Every run now generates tests against the same explicit contract. The same guidance warns that examples are reference points to check against, not the whole specification. So combine them with a request for general-purpose handling of all valid inputs.

Each incorrect approach is a familiar trap. Stronger wording in the written instruction raises priority without adding information, so the ambiguity remains. Running generation several times and keeping the tests that agree adds latency and cost, and the runs may still agree on a wrong interpretation. Self-rated confidence is poorly calibrated: a model can give high confidence to every one of its conflicting interpretations. When output varies because the prompt does not specify the goal clearly enough, the fix is always to make the goal concrete.

See Claude prompting best practices and Claude Code common workflows for guidance on examples and edge-case test generation.

QUESTION: The code review system uses an extraction tool whose "input_schema" marks "cwe_id" as a required string in every finding. For non-security findings, Claude fills the field with plausible but invented identifiers. Which schema change best eliminates these fabricated values?
answers: Add a validation-retry loop that returns fabricated identifiers to Claude with an error message.
Enable "strict: true" on the tool definition so inputs always conform exactly to the schema.
Add a system prompt rule telling Claude never to invent an identifier for non-security findings.
Make "cwe_id" nullable so Claude can return null when no identifier applies.
feedbacks: Retry with error feedback works for format and structural mistakes. But it cannot help when the correct information does not exist for the finding. A non-security finding has no real CWE identifier, so each retry would only produce another invented value.

Strict tool use guarantees that tool inputs are syntactically valid against the schema. But in this case the schema already requires a string for every finding. Enforcing that requirement more strictly does not stop fabrication, because the field would still have to contain some string, invented or not.

A prompt instruction cannot override the schema, which still requires a string value in every finding. Claude must emit something for the required field, so the instruction conflicts with the structure that Claude is asked to produce, and the fabrication continues.

When a schema requires a field that the source material does not always support, the model tends to invent a value to satisfy the schema. Making the field optional or nullable gives Claude a legitimate way to signal that the value is absent. This removes the reason to invent identifiers for non-security findings.
prompt.explanation:
This question is about a core schema design principle for extraction tools: mark a field as required only when the source really always contains it. A JSON schema is not only a format contract. It also pushes the model's generation in a direction. If the schema requires a string in cwe_id for every finding, Claude will produce one even when no real identifier exists, because the alternative is to break the structure it was asked to follow. For this reason, Anthropic's guidance for extraction schemas is to make fields optional or nullable (for example, allowing both string and null types) whenever the information may legitimately be absent. This gives the model an honest way to say "not applicable" instead of hallucinating a value.

Each of the other approaches misses the root cause. Setting strict: true uses grammar-constrained sampling to guarantee that the tool input matches the schema. That is the right fix for malformed JSON or missing required fields. But in this case the schema itself is what forces the bad value, and strict conformance to a flawed schema only makes the fabrication more reliable. A prompt rule against inventing identifiers asks the model to do something that its required schema does not allow, so the model cannot follow it consistently. A validation-retry loop helps only when the model made a mistake that can be corrected. It is documented as ineffective when the required information is not in the source, and that is the case for a non-security finding with no CWE.

In general, structure problems (invalid JSON, wrong types) are solved with enforcement mechanisms like strict tool use. Truthfulness problems (invented values) are solved with schema honesty, such as nullable fields, enums that include "unclear", and an "other" option combined with a detail string. See Strict tool use and Define tools for the documented limits of each mechanism.

QUESTION: The engineer who configured the automated reviews stored the team's review criteria in their own "~/.claude/CLAUDE.md". Reviews on their laptop follow the criteria, but pipeline runs ignore them and produce unfocused feedback. What should the engineer do?
answers: Add the review criteria to the committed ".claude/settings.json" so the pipeline applies them.
Run /memory at the start of each CI job so the engineer's memory files are loaded.
Rewrite the CI prompt to tell Claude to review more conservatively and stay focused.
Move the review criteria into the project root CLAUDE.md and commit it to the repository.
feedbacks: The settings.json files hold JSON configuration, such as permission rules and tool settings. They do not hold lasting written instructions. Review criteria are behavioral guidance, so they belong in a CLAUDE.md file, not in settings.

The /memory command views and edits the memory files that are available in the current environment. It cannot import a file from a different user's home directory. The CI runner has no copy of the engineer's user-level file, so there is nothing for it to load.

Vague wording, like asking Claude to be more conservative, produces inconsistent results and does not provide the concrete criteria that the team defined. The root cause is that the criteria never reach the CI environment, not that the prompt lacks emphasis.

A user-level CLAUDE.md is stored in one person's home directory and is never shared through version control, so the CI environment never loads it. When the criteria are committed at the project level, every checkout, including the pipeline's, provides the same review context.
prompt.explanation:
Claude Code reads instructions from several locations, and each location has a different audience. User instructions in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md apply to one person across all of their projects. They are stored outside the repository, so version control never carries them anywhere. Project instructions in a root CLAUDE.md (or .claude/CLAUDE.md) are committed, so they reach anyone, or anything, that checks out the code. A CI runner acts like another user with its own clean environment. It gets only what the repository contains, and nothing from any engineer's home directory. That is why the reviews were correct on the engineer's laptop, where the user-level file was loaded, and lost focus in the pipeline, where it was not.

The repository is the only reliable way to deliver shared context. Testing standards, fixture conventions, and review criteria that an automated pipeline depends on must be committed at the project level. Then every invocation, human or automated, starts from the same instructions. Each of the other approaches misses this. .claude/settings.json is a JSON settings file for permissions and tool configuration, not a place for written instructions. Stronger prompt wording, like asking for conservative reviews, is vague guidance that cannot replace the explicit criteria. And /memory only shows the memory files that are already present in the environment. On a CI runner, these do not include anyone's personal ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md.

See Manage Claude's memory for the user, project, and local instruction scopes, and The .claude directory for which files are committed and shared versus personal.

QUESTION: Before adding a complex new test-generation stage to the pipeline, the team had Claude interview them about edge cases, concerns, and tradeoffs, and the interview is now complete. According to Anthropic's recommended Claude Code workflow, what should happen next?
answers: Continue implementing in the same session, since the interview answers are already loaded into context.
Run /compact to summarize the interview transcript, then implement within the compacted session.
Repeat the interview in plan mode so the answers become a plan the team can formally approve.
Have Claude write the full spec to a "SPEC.md" file, then implement it in a fresh session.
feedbacks: Keeping the interview transcript in context mixes a long question-and-answer exchange with the implementation work. This reduces attention on the decisions that matter. The recommended workflow records the decisions in a written spec and then starts with a clean context for the implementation.

Compaction summarizes the history to free context, but the summary can lose precise details. It is also not the documented next step of the interview pattern. Writing the decisions to a spec file keeps them word for word and makes them reusable.

Plan mode is a related but separate technique for researching and proposing changes without editing files. The interview has already brought out the design decisions, so running it again adds overhead. The next documented step is to write the spec and implement from it.

The documented interview workflow ends with Claude writing a complete spec, which can be understood on its own, to a file such as SPEC.md. Starting a fresh session for the implementation gives Claude a clean context that is focused on the written spec, not on the long interview transcript.
prompt.explanation:
The interview pattern, which Anthropic documents as Let Claude interview you, has two halves, and this question tests the second one. The first half is the interview itself. Claude asks about technical implementation, edge cases, concerns, and tradeoffs, and it asks in detail about the hard parts that the developer may not have considered. The second half is turning those answers into a lasting document. Claude writes a complete spec to a file such as SPEC.md, and the team then starts a fresh session to implement it.

The fresh session matters because of how context works. After a long interview, the conversation holds dozens of question-and-answer turns, false starts, and options that were reconsidered. If you implement in that same session, the model has to weigh all of it, while a written spec keeps only the final decisions. A good spec can be understood on its own. It names the files and interfaces involved, states what is out of scope, and ends with an end-to-end verification step. A clean session can then carry it out without working out the reasoning again.

Each alternative fails in a specific way. Continuing in the same session keeps the long, mixed transcript as the source of truth. Running /compact produces a summary that loses information and can drop precise details, and it was never the documented next step of this pattern. Running the interview again in plan mode confuses two related techniques. Plan mode controls permissions (research without edits until a plan is approved), while the interview pattern is about requirements discovery. Once the interview is done, repeating it gains nothing.

See Claude Code Best Practices for the interview-to-spec workflow and Permission Modes for how plan mode differs.

QUESTION: The root CLAUDE.md contains 150 lines of test-generation conventions. Test files are spread across the repository, next to the code they test. Reviews of pull requests that change no test files still load those lines. What restructuring fixes this?
answers: Place a directory-level CLAUDE.md containing the conventions inside every folder that holds test files.
Keep the conventions in CLAUDE.md but import them with "@standards/test-conventions.md" from a separate file.
Move the conventions into a ".claude/rules/" file with "paths" frontmatter globs matching the test files.
Add a CLAUDE.md instruction telling Claude to apply the test conventions only when a pull request changes tests.
feedbacks: Test files are placed next to the source code across the whole repository. So this would require copying the conventions into a large number of directories and keeping every copy the same. Path-scoped rules with glob patterns are the documented approach when a convention applies to a file type in many locations.

Imports organize content into separate files, but imported files are expanded and loaded into context at launch. Every session, including reviews of non-test changes, would still load all 150 lines. This changes how the content is maintained, but it does not reduce context usage.

A rule file with a paths glob in its YAML frontmatter (the settings block at the top of the file) is loaded only when Claude Code works with files that match the pattern. The test files are spread out next to the code they cover. A glob that uses ** with the test file extensions limits the conventions to that file type in any location. Runs that never touch tests never pay the context cost.

An instruction about when to apply the conventions does not change what is loaded. The 150 lines still enter the context of every session. The problem described is context usage, and only conditional loading addresses it.
prompt.explanation:
The .claude/rules/ directory exists so that project instructions can be split into focused files. Its key capability is conditional loading. A rule file whose YAML frontmatter (the settings block at the top of the file) includes a paths field with glob patterns is loaded into context only when Claude Code actually works with a matching file, for example when it reads, writes, or edits that file. A rule without paths is loaded at launch for every session, in the same way as CLAUDE.md itself. So the frontmatter is what turns a separate file into one that saves tokens.

Everything in the root CLAUDE.md, and anything it imports, is a fixed cost for every session. The @path/to/import syntax only organizes content. Imported files are expanded in place when the session starts, so moving content into an import does not reduce what is loaded. In the same way, a written instruction to "only apply these rules for test changes" is applied after the conventions are already in context, so the tokens are used either way. Directory-level CLAUDE.md files do load conditionally, but they tie conventions to specific folders. This does not work well when the relevant files (in this case, tests placed next to the source) are spread across the entire repository. Path scoping based on globs matches by file type in any location and keeps the conventions in a single place.

Remember one limit: path-scoped rules reduce context, but they do not provide enforcement. Claude treats rule files as instructions, so anything that must never be skipped belongs in a hook, not in a rule file. See Manage Claude's memory and Context windows for how rules load and how they behave across a session.
